docs.title: Mujou
docs.text:
Asynchronous Distributed Deep Learning Library for Continuous Learning

Image: a new work based on Yoichi Ochiai's Liquid Universe.

Mujou is a deep learning framework that keeps inferring and learning at the same time. You write nodes in PyTorch code and run a network that connects them.

Early development

Mujou is in an early stage of development. The API may change without notice.

docs.title: 🌱 A network that keeps learning
docs.text:
Conventional machine learning trains a model, then freezes its weights for inference. A Mujou network takes input and produces output for as long as it runs, and keeps learning at the same time.

There is no mode to switch between training and inference, and there are no epochs.

The name comes from 無常 (mujō, impermanence: nothing stays the same), as in the Buddhist phrase 諸行無常. Mujou is a framework for machines that keep learning from a stream and keep changing. It targets uses that learn while they act, such as real-time processing and robotics.

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🔄 Inference and learning at once: no training mode, no inference mode, no epochs
  • 🧩 Nodes in PyTorch: write each node in ordinary PyTorch code, run synchronously inside the node
  • ⚡ Asynchronous nodes: each node updates on a thread of its own and never waits for another
  • ⏱️ Continuous time: nodes update in proportion to dt, the time that really passed
  • 💾 State without stopping: take the state of a running network and run again from it later
  • 🧪 Deterministic tests: a virtual timer and manual updates for testing nodes

docs.text:

Each node repeats its update on a thread of its own and never waits for another node; it reads the latest value its neighbor sent.

The host (the program that runs the network) writes inputs to the running network and reads its outputs.

docs.title: 🚀 The smallest program
docs.text:
The program below runs a network of two nodes that computes \(y = 2x + 1\) and reads the output. The Quickstart explains what it does.

examples/quickstart.py 
"""The smallest program: two nodes in a network, run in the background.

The host writes an input, follows the output until it arrives and stops.
"""

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((3,))  # every message here is a float32 vector of 3


class Scale(Node):
    """Sends its input times ``factor``."""

    def __init__(self, factor: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.factor = factor
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous side
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next side

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # the latest input; never waits
        self.next.send(self.factor * x)


class Shift(Node):
    """Sends its input plus ``offset``."""

    def __init__(self, offset: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.offset = offset
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.prev.recv() + self.offset)


class Affine(mujou.Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Scale(2.0)
        self.shift = Shift(1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev = self.scale.prev  # the input of the network
        self.next = self.shift.next  # the output of the network




net = Affine()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on threads of their own until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})  # the unconnected input port of scale
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
assert torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1)

docs.title: 🧠 How Mujou Works
docs.text:
This page explains the ideas behind Mujou. It covers five of them.

  • Nodes: the units of computation
  • Ports and channels: the connection points of nodes and the connections between them
  • Networks: how nodes are put together
  • Global time: the flow of time that every node follows
  • State: what you can take from a running network and put back later

How to write the code is in the User Guide.

        A["Node A"] <-->|Channel| B["Node B"] <-->|Channel| C["Node C"]
    end
    T["The run's timer"]
    H -->|"through the Run that mujou.run(net) returns: write inputs, read outputs, take the state"| N
    T -.->|"time and dt"| N

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
A node is the unit of computation. You write a node as a class that inherits from mujou.Node.

Inside a node, ordinary PyTorch code runs synchronously. It may even use backpropagation (BP), as long as the BP stays inside the node.

Between nodes, everything is asynchronous. Mujou calls the node's on_update(dt) over and over on a thread of its own, and a node never waits for another node. In each on_update, the node does three things.

  1. It reads the latest values its neighbors sent
  2. It updates its state
  3. It sends its results

Mujou owns the loop, so a node holds no while loop of its own. Mujou also calls other hooks that a node can override, for example when the run starts and stops; their order is in the API reference of Node.

There are no epochs, no switch between training and inference, and no hook called for each received message.

The node class decides how much computation one node holds: one layer, or several layers, or a whole model. The node boundaries are the asynchronous boundaries. To compute several layers synchronously, put them in one node class. The same holds when several layers should learn together with BP.

The three rules a node keeps

  • No graphs across nodes: it does not join computation graphs across nodes. A value is detached from the computation graph when it is sent, so gradients never pass between nodes
  • Only through ports: it talks to other nodes and to the host only through its own ports
  • Time is read-only: it only reads the time. Only the host moves the time

If a node raises an exception, the whole run stops. Mujou never stops only the node that raised and keeps the others running (see Errors and Shutdown).

The default update rule will be PC-ALM (Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding; not implemented yet), where each node learns with local updates only. Update rules are not built into Mujou: a node can use any rule that keeps to the rules above.

docs.title: Ports and channels
docs.text:
A port is a connection point that a node holds. A channel is one connection between two ports, made by connect.

A channel has one slot for the value in each direction, and only the sender in that direction writes the slot.

A port declares what it sends and what it receives, as a shape and a dtype. Two ports connect only when the type that each sends matches the type that the other receives. Mujou checks this when you call connect, and converts no dtype.

Reading and writing work like this.

  • No waiting: a reader gets the latest value at that moment. It never waits for a new value
  • No queue: a value may be overwritten before anyone reads it, and the same value may be read many times. Both are normal
  • Initial value: before the sender has written, the reader gets the initial value of the sender's port (zeros by default). has_received() tells whether the sender has written yet
  • A copy: every value is a copy of a torch.Tensor, detached from the computation graph. Changing a received tensor affects no other node
  • With its time: every value carries the time it was sent. To tell whether a value is new, read it with its time (recv_with_time()) and compare that time with the time of the value read last. If the time has moved on, the value is new

A port may connect to several peers. It then receives one value per channel, and the node decides how to combine them (sum, average, ...).

A port may also stay unconnected. Unconnected ports are the inputs and outputs of the network.

  • The host writes input to an unconnected input port. The written value stays there until the host writes again
  • The host can read the latest value that any sending port sent. This covers not only unconnected output ports but also ports that connect nodes

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
A network declares how nodes are put together. You write it as a class that inherits from mujou.Network, much like giving a PyTorch nn.Module its child modules. You build it in three steps.

  1. Hold nodes, or other networks, as attributes
  2. Connect their ports with connect
  3. Expose the ports that should connect from outside as the network's own attributes

A network that exposes ports connects to other nodes and networks just like a node does.

A network is used only for building. It has no hooks and runs nothing itself. While running, the nodes inside it each run on their own, so wrapping nodes in a network does not synchronize them.

mujou.run(net) checks the structure and the types, freezes it, and runs it. After that, no connection can be added.

Each node is named by its path, the attribute names from the root joined with ., such as "body.l1". The state uses these paths.

Renaming breaks restoring

Renaming an attribute or changing a connection makes a state taken before the change impossible to restore.

docs.title: Global time
docs.text:
Mujou treats a learning network as a system that changes continuously over time. dt is the time in seconds since the node's last update.

A node updates its state in proportion to dt. For a state \(x\) that follows \(\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x)\), one update is this (explicit Euler).

x = x + dt * f(x)

Nodes update at different rates, and their rates vary with the load. If the update size were fixed per iteration, a faster node would change its state more. With updates proportional to dt, every node follows the same dynamics on the same flow of time; a higher load only makes dt longer.

Do not cap dt

Do not cap dt, because a capped dt drops time that really passed. If a large dt makes the update unstable, split it into smaller steps inside one on_update.

Every node has a period, 0.01 s by default. The interval between two updates varies, but on average the node updates once every period. When the node is late, dt is longer than the period. dt is the time that actually passed, so update in proportion to dt even with a period set.

Each run has one timer, and every node of the run and the host use it. By default, it is the global timer, one per process. The host can make the time run faster or slower than real time. Nodes only read the time.

The host waits with mujou.time.sleep

To wait on that time, for example to show an input for two seconds, the host uses mujou.time.sleep, not the standard time.sleep, which waits in real time.

To take the state of a running network, Mujou pauses the run and stops its timer. The paused time does not enter any dt after the run resumes, so to the nodes it is as if the pause never happened.

A pause stops the time of every run that uses the same timer; give a run its own timer to keep it apart (see Controlling Time).

A pause is for taking the state and for observing. Do not make pausing part of how the network learns.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
You can take the state of a running network without ending the run, and later run the network again from that state. The state is one tree that holds:

  • the state of each node (weights, activities, and other tensors), by node path
  • the latest value in each slot, with its time
  • the time of each node's last update, and the time of the timer

The values in the slots are part of the state because a network is its nodes together with the values flowing between them. If they went back to their initial values, the neighbors would leave the equilibrium they had reached.

A node collects its own state, as nn.Module does: tensors and nn.Modules assigned to its attributes go into the state automatically.

Taking the state causes the pause described in the previous section. Each node pauses not in the middle of on_update but after one update ends and before the next begins, so every value in the tree belongs to the same moment.

When you take the state What you get While the network runs The state at that moment After a normal end The values as the nodes left them after on_stop After an exception Nothing: it raises NetworkError. Take the state you want to keep while the network runs

In the tree taken after a normal end, the timer's time is the later of two: when shutdown() asked the run to stop, and when a node last updated or sent. A run restored from this tree does not count the time that passed after the end.

Do not change the state in on_stop

Because the tree after a normal end is taken after on_stop, a change that on_stop makes to the state goes into that tree. For example, self.w = None in on_stop removes w from it. Do not change the state in on_stop; release only resources such as I/O there.

To restore, pass the tree as mujou.run(net, state=tree). The network goes on from the time the tree was taken, with the same node states and slot values. The network must have the same node paths and connections as the one the tree was taken from.

Storing the tree in a file (torch.save, pickle, ...) is up to you. See Saving and Restoring State.

docs.title: mujou.Network
docs.text:
Network()

Bases: Component

A composite of nodes and other networks, declared as attributes.

Assign nodes and networks as attributes, connect their ports with Port.connect, and expose the ports the outside should reach as attributes of the network (by convention prev and next for the previous and the next side, e.g. self.prev = self.l1.prev). The network registers what is assigned, as nn.Module registers submodules, so nodes and networks in lists or dicts are not part of it. A network is a build-time structure: its nodes still run independently and asynchronously.

Call super().__init__() before assigning a node, a network or a port. Declare ports as instance attributes (in __init__), not class attributes, and do not use the names of the methods below for attributes.

mujou.run(net) builds the network (build) and runs it; the Run it returns is how the host talks to the running nodes.

Example::

class Stack(Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.l1 = Hidden(784, 256)
        self.l2 = Hidden(256, 256)
        self.l1.next.connect(self.l2.prev)
        self.prev = self.l1.prev  # expose the previous side
        self.next = self.l2.next  # expose the next side


class Classifier(Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.body = Stack()
        self.head = Head()  # a node with prev, next and teacher ports
        self.body.next.connect(self.head.prev)  # l2.next <-> head.prev
        self.prev = self.body.prev  # the input
        self.teacher = self.head.teacher  # the target, a port of head


net = Classifier()
with mujou.run(net, inputs={net.prev: x0, net.teacher: y0}) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x, net.teacher: y})  # switch together
    mujou.time.sleep(0.1)  # present the input for 0.1 s of global time
    prediction = run.read(net.head.next)
    state = run.state_dict()

docs.title: build
docs.text:
build() -> Graph

Check the structure of this network as the root, freeze it and return its graph.

After build, no port in the tree takes new connections, and no part of the tree, this network included, can become part of a bigger network: build only the network you will run. Calling it again returns the same graph. mujou.run calls it.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

Part of the tree (a node, a network or a port) belongs to another built network, or this network is part of a built one.

ValueError

The structure is invalid: the tree has no node; a component appears at two paths; a port is owned by two nodes (or under two names); a port is declared as a class attribute; a network exposes a port that no node inside it owns; or a channel leads to a port outside the tree.

docs.title: mujou.Group
docs.text:
Group(*components: Node | Network, **named: Node | Network)

Bases: Network

A network of the given nodes and networks side by side, unconnected unless they were connected before.

One given by position is at the path of its position ("0", "1", ...) and one given by keyword at its keyword, so the node l1 of Group(a, b) is "1.l1" in b and that of Group(enc=a) is "enc.l1"; a node n in Group(n, a) is "0", as if it were an attribute "0" of a network. Group(n) of one component still puts it at "0". mujou.run(a, b) runs Group(a, b); mujou.run(a) runs a alone as the root.

Example::

enc, dec = Encoder(), Decoder()
enc.next.connect(dec.prev)
with mujou.run(Group(enc=enc, dec=dec)) as run:
    state = run.state_dict()  # nodes "enc.l1", ..., "dec.l1", ...
RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

A value is neither a Node nor a Network.

ValueError

A keyword is empty, holds a . (a path would be ambiguous), starts with _, is the name of an attribute of Network (such as build), or is the path of a position.

Graph()

The structure of a built network (or of a node run alone): what runs when mujou.run runs it.

Network.build makes it, and mujou.run for a node given alone; it cannot be created directly, and mujou.run takes nodes and networks, not graphs. It is a different object from the network it was built from: the network declares the structure, and the graph is what runs. A graph runs once.

docs.title: mujou.run
docs.text:
run(
    component: Node | Network,
    *components: Node | Network,
    timer: Timer | None = None,
    inputs: Mapping[P, Tensor | Mapping[str, object]] | None = None,
    state: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> Run

Build the given nodes and networks and run them in the background; return once every node has started.

One component alone is the root of the run: a network runs as it is (its nodes at "l1", ...), and a node is at the path "" with its ports at "prev", "next", .... Several run as Group(component, *components), nodes and networks mixed or not, so their paths start with their positions: "0" for a node given first, "1.l1", ... for the nodes of a network given second. Either way the host writes and reads the ports themselves (run.write({node.prev: x})).

Every node's thread is set up, on_start (and, with state, the node's load_state_dict) has returned, and the run's timer runs when this returns. A network or node runs once.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION component

The node or network to run.

TYPE: Node | Network

components

More nodes and networks to run with it.

TYPE: Node | Network DEFAULT: ()

timer

The time axis of the run: every node's dt, every message's time and every pause of the run is on it. None is the global timer, which mujou.time reads and every run without a timer of its own shares.

TYPE: Timer | None DEFAULT: None

inputs

The initial values of unconnected single-peer ports that receive, as Run.write takes them. Written after state, they replace its values and carry its time.

TYPE: Mapping[P, Tensor | Mapping[str, object]] | None DEFAULT: None

state

A tree from Run.state_dict to restore: the StateDict, or any mapping of the same items (such as a plain dict). The slots, the nodes' states (through each node's load_state_dict, after its on_start), their last update times and the timer continue from the time the tree was taken. Build the networks as the ones the tree came from: the same node paths and slots.

TYPE: Mapping[str, Any] | None DEFAULT: None

Example, with the node Error of the example of Run::

node = Error()
with mujou.run(node, inputs={node.prev: torch.ones(2)}) as run:
    mujou.time.sleep(0.1)
    error = run.read(node.next)
RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

A network or node has already run ("Leaky has already run; create a new instance to run again"), or part of one belongs to another network that was built but has not run; or this is called from a node's hook.

TypeError

A value is neither a Node nor a Network.

(ValueError, TypeError)

As Network.build, Group and Run.write (for inputs) raise; state does not match the networks, or the timer it would set back has another run on it. Nothing has started: the same networks, given the same way, may run once the cause is gone.

NetworkError

A node raised while starting; the run has stopped.

docs.title: mujou.Run
docs.text:
Run()

A run of networks, as mujou.run returns it: what the host uses to talk to the running nodes.

The nodes run in the background, each on its own thread; the host's thread only writes inputs, reads outputs and takes the state:

  • write inputs, read / read_with_time / subscribe outputs, take a state_dict.
  • shutdown() to stop the run, or join() to wait until it stops.
  • After a normal end: take the final state_dict.

A with statement shuts the run down at its end. These methods are for the host: calling them from a node's hook raises RuntimeError.

If a node raises, the whole run stops. If that happens while mujou.run starts the nodes, mujou.run raises NetworkError; otherwise every later call of write, read, read_with_time, subscribe (and its iterator), state_dict, shutdown and join raises it. Its __cause__ is the node's exception. The state at the exception is not kept.

A run keeps running when the host drops it, until shutdown or, at the latest, the interpreter's exit (which waits for on_stop). At the exit, the runs start stopping once the main thread has ended, before the interpreter joins the non-daemon threads, and the exit waits until they have stopped.

Example::

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NextPort, Node, Port, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((2,))


class Error(Node):  # sends its input minus its teacher
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.teacher = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.prev.recv() - self.teacher.recv())


node = Error()
x, y = torch.ones(2), torch.zeros(2)
with mujou.run(node, inputs={node.prev: x, node.teacher: y}) as run:
    run.write({node.prev: 2 * x, node.teacher: x})  # switch together
    mujou.time.sleep(0.1)  # present the input for 0.1 s of global time
    error, t = run.read_with_time(node.next)
state = run.state_dict()  # the state at the end, to save

docs.title: timer property
docs.text:
timer: Timer

The run's timer: the timer given to mujou.run, or the global timer (the one mujou.time reads) when none was given.

Every node's dt and every time of the run is on it.

docs.title: write
docs.text:
write(values: Mapping[P, Tensor | Mapping[str, object]]) -> Timestamp

Write messages to unconnected single-peer ports that receive, and return the time they carry.

The values are detached and copied. All of them switch together and carry the same time: at any one moment, a node sees either all of them or none. (A node that reads two of them one after the other may still see a later write in between; compare the times to tell.) Any port of the tree can be written, exposed by the root or not.

The time is the run's timer at the write, as a node's recv_with_time and the /in slots of state_dict show it; read_with_time shows the times of sends, not of writes. An empty values changes nothing and returns the time all the same.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

The run has stopped normally (no node reads what is written then).

ValueError

A port is outside the run, connected, takes many peers, or receives nothing; or a shape or the keys differ.

TypeError

A message or dtype differs from the spec.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: read
docs.text:
read(port: Port[S, Any, Any]) -> S

Return the latest message port sent.

Any port that sends can be read, so a connected port shows an inner node. Only send (to every peer) updates the value read here; before the first one it is the port's initial (zeros by default) or the value restored from state. The tensors are new copies on the CPU. read_with_time also returns the time it was sent at.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

port is outside the run or sends nothing.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: read_with_time
docs.text:
read_with_time(port: Port[S, Any, Any]) -> tuple[S, Timestamp]

Return the latest message port sent, as read does, and the time it was sent at.

The time is on the run's timer. A Timestamp does not say which timer it is on: compare it only with times of the same timer (with mujou.time only when the run is on the global timer).

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

port is outside the run or sends nothing.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.title: subscribe
docs.text:
subscribe(
    port: Port[S, Any, Any], timeout: float = math.inf
) -> Iterator[tuple[S, Timestamp]]

Iterate over the messages port sends, with their times.

The first step yields the latest message at the time of this call (before the first send, the port's initial or the restored value) without waiting. Each later step waits until a newer message is sent and yields the latest; messages sent in between are skipped. Only the consumer waits: the sending node never does. The iterator ends when the run shuts down normally. Shut the run down before the program ends: without a timeout, a thread iterating here ends only with the run. In a ManualRun nothing is sent unless step is called, so a wait here without a timeout on the thread that steps never ends.

To wait for one message that meets a condition, use wait_for.

The port to follow.

TYPE: Port[S, Any, Any]

timeout

Real seconds, counted from this call, that the whole iteration may take, the time spent in the loop's body included. math.inf iterates as long as the run runs.

TimeoutError

The run stopped because a node raised (also from the iterator).

node = Error()
x = torch.ones(2)
with mujou.run(node, inputs={node.prev: x}) as run:

docs.title: state_dict
docs.text:
state_dict(timeout: float = 30.0) -> StateDict

Copy the state of the run at one time, while it runs or after it ended normally.

While it runs, this pauses the run's timer and nodes, copies the state and resumes, and returns once the run has resumed. It waits at most timeout for every node to pause. After a normal end, this copies the state as the nodes left it, calling each node's state_dict on this thread (an exception it raises reaches the caller as it is). The tree's timer holds the time at which shutdown asked the run to stop, as if the run had paused then (or a later update or send of an on_stop), so that a restored run goes on from there without the time that passed after the end.

The tree is a copy (later updates of the nodes do not change it), a StateDict (a dict) that pickles; saving it is up to the host. Pass it to mujou.run(..., state=tree) to restore it::

{
    "nodes": {"body.l1": ..., ...},  # each node's state_dict()
    "slots": {"body.l1.next/out": (value, time_ns, sent), ...},
    "last_update_ns": {"body.l1": int, ...},
    "timer": {"time_ns": int, "scale": float},
}

A node is keyed by its attribute path from the root. A slot is keyed by the path of the port through its owning node ("body.l1.prev/in", not an exposed name such as "prev/in") and holds its latest message: /out what read returns, /ch0, /ch1, ... each channel, and /in what the host wrote. A node run alone is the root: it is keyed "" and its slots "prev/in", "next/out", ....

The tensors of the tree stay on their nodes' devices. tree.cpu() moves them all to the CPU, for example before saving the tree.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION timeout

Real seconds to wait for every node to pause (the end of its current on_update): finite and > 0. After the end there is nothing to wait for, and it is only checked.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 30.0

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

This is called from a node's hook.

ValueError

timeout is not finite and > 0.

PauseTimeoutError

A node did not pause within timeout; no state is taken and the run keeps running.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised; its state is not kept.

docs.title: mujou.Node
docs.text:
Node(*, device: device | str = 'cpu', seed: int | None = None, period: float = 0.01)

Bases: Node, Component

A unit of asynchronous computation: the leaf of a network.

Declare the ports as instance attributes in __init__, after super().__init__() (build rejects ports declared on the class). The node registers them as they are assigned. A node must not hold other nodes or networks as attributes (assigning one raises ValueError); put them side by side in a Network instead.

Override the lifecycle hooks below; each does nothing by default, except state_dict and load_state_dict. As in any subclass, call super().__init__() first in __init__ and the same hook of super() first in each override. The framework calls the hooks on the node's own thread, except state_dict:

  • on_thread_start(): once, right before on_start, after the framework has set up the thread (see below). Make the node's own per-thread settings here.
  • on_start(): once, when the network runs (also when it was restored). Allocate and initialize the state here.
  • load_state_dict(state): only when the network was restored, after on_start and before the first on_update. state is a copy of what this node's state_dict returned. By default it copies the state into the collected tensors and modules (see below). When device is CUDA, the framework waits for the node's stream after it.
  • on_update(dt): repeatedly, once every period on average (see below). dt is the time in seconds on the run's timer since the node's last update. Read the ports with recv, update in proportion to dt, and write the ports with send. It never waits for other nodes.
  • on_pause(): when the node has stopped for a pause of the network (as Run.state_dict does). on_resume(): when the pause ends, before the next on_update.
  • on_exception(): once on every node, when a hook of any node has raised, before on_stop.
  • on_stop(): once, when the network stops, also after an exception. It must not change what state_dict returns: the state taken after a normal end is the state at the stop.
  • state_dict(): when the network's state is taken, on the runtime's control thread while the node is paused (or, after a normal end, on the host's thread that called Run.state_dict), so recv and send raise RuntimeError there. Return the node's own state as a picklable object; it may hold the live tensors, because the framework copies it before the node resumes. By default it returns the collected tensors and modules (see below).

The node collects its state by itself, as nn.Module does: every attribute assigned a torch.Tensor (nn.Parameter included) or an nn.Module, whether or not its name starts with _, is registered under its name. Assigning any other value (None too) under that name, or del, removes it. Ports, numbers, lists and dicts of tensors are not collected, and neither are properties (what a setter stores is, under its own name). The default state_dict and load_state_dict save and restore what is registered; override both to choose the state yourself (they may call super()). Allocate the tensors of the state by on_start and update them in place afterwards: the default load_state_dict copies into them in place.

If any hook raises, the whole network stops. A hook must not call mujou.run or the methods of any Run (write, read, state_dict, ...): they raise RuntimeError there, because a node talks only through its own ports.

Before on_start, the framework sets up the node's thread: it turns off gradient recording (to backpropagate inside the node, wrap the forward computation and backward in with torch.enable_grad(): marked # mujou: local-autograd), creates generator from seed on device, and, when device is CUDA, makes the device and a stream of the node's own current. On CUDA it also waits for that stream after on_update, after load_state_dict and around state_dict. It does this in hooks of its own, whose names start with _: do not override those, and overriding a public hook never skips them.

The node updates once every period (0.01 s by default) of the run's timer on average: the time an update takes counts toward the period, and a node that falls a whole period behind does not update several times in a row to catch up. A pause does not count. dt is still the time that actually passed since the last update, longer than period when the node is late, so keep updating in proportion to it and stay stable for the longest dt it can get. A manual run (ManualRun.step) ignores the period.

period=0.0 updates as soon as any time has passed since the last update. Set it only when the node must: such a node keeps a CPU core busy, and takes time from the other nodes, whose dt it makes irregular.

device, generator, period and timer (the reading side of the run's timer) are reserved names: do not assign attributes of those names (a class attribute period makes the run raise TypeError).

Example::

class Hidden(Node):
    def __init__(self, n_in: int, n_out: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(seed=0)
        x, h = TensorSpec((32, n_in)), TensorSpec((32, n_out))
        # Send W^T eps back and receive x from the previous side (one peer).
        self.prev = PrevPort(send=x, recv=x)
        # Send h forward and receive W^T eps from each next peer (many).
        self.next = NextPort(send=h, recv=h)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # torch.Tensor
        feedback = self.next.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor]
        ...
        self.next.send(h)
        self.prev.send(wt_eps)


l1, l2 = Hidden(784, 256), Hidden(256, 256)
l1.next.connect(l2.prev)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION device

Where the node computes: the CPU or a CUDA device (no other device type is supported). Received messages arrive on it. "cuda" without an index is fixed to the host's current CUDA device.

TYPE: device | str DEFAULT: 'cpu'

seed

The seed of generator. None seeds it nondeterministically.

TYPE: int | None DEFAULT: None

period

The time between two updates on average, in seconds of the run's timer. 0.0 updates as soon as any time has passed.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 0.01

RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

period is None or a bool.

ValueError

device is neither the CPU nor a CUDA device, or is CUDA while CUDA is not available, or period is negative or not finite.

docs.text:
Port(
    send: MessageSpec[S] | None = None,
    recv: MessageSpec[R] | None = None,
    *,
    multi: bool = False,
    initial: S | None = None,
)

A connection point that sends messages of type S and receives R.

Declare ports as attributes of a node (or expose a port of a child as an attribute of a network). send is the spec of what this port sends and recv the spec of what it receives; either may be omitted for a one-way port (omit it: type checkers reject None and infer Never for an omitted spec). multi=True lets the port take any number of peers (Multi) and multi=False at most one (Single). The default is one peer for Port and PrevPort, and many for NextPort. multi fixes what recv returns: the message for one peer, a dict keyed by Channel for many.

Two ports connect when the send of each equals the recv of the other (an omitted spec matches an omitted spec). A port may stay unconnected.

initial is what the port has sent before its first send: what its peers receive and the host reads until then. It must match send exactly, and is copied when the port is made. Without it, that is the zeros() of send. A restored run takes the values from the state instead.

Once assigned as an attribute of a node, the port is named "<node class>.<attribute>" (e.g. "Shift.next") in errors and its repr; the first assignment names it.

PrevPort and NextPort are ports with other defaults for the number of peers, for the previous and the next side of a node by convention.

Example::

class Sensor(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.out = Port(send=TensorSpec((3,)), initial=torch.ones(3))


class Monitor(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.inp = Port(recv=TensorSpec((3,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.inp.recv()  # torch.Tensor (one peer); ones until out sends


sensor, monitor = Sensor(), Monitor()
sensor.out.connect(monitor.inp)

docs.title: mujou.testing
docs.text:
Deterministic tests of nodes and networks.

Run the networks with run, which puts them on a new VirtualTimer, advance the timer by a fixed dt and step the nodes by hand in a fixed order: every update then sees exactly that dt, and the result can be compared with the discrete algorithm. Mujou tests its own nodes with the same API.

Example::

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
import mujou.testing
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec


class Double(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=TensorSpec((2,)))
        self.next = NextPort(send=TensorSpec((2,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(2 * self.prev.recv())


class Chain(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = Double(), Double()
        self.a.next.connect(self.b.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.a.prev, self.b.next


net = Chain()
x = torch.ones(2)
with mujou.testing.run(net, inputs={net.prev: x}) as run:
    run.timer.advance(0.001)  # the run's VirtualTimer
    run.step(net.a, net.b)  # a, then b reads a's new value
    y, t = run.read_with_time(net.next)
assert torch.equal(y, 4 * x) and t.ns == 1_000_000

A run whose nodes update only when step lets them, for tests.

mujou.testing.run returns it. The nodes start and stop as in any run, but between updates each waits for step. On a VirtualTimer (the default), every dt is then exactly the time the test advanced with timer.advance, and the result follows the discrete algorithm of the chosen order.

docs.title: step
docs.text:
step(*nodes: Node) -> None

Update each of nodes once, one after another in the given order (by default every node, in the order of the tree), and return when done.

step does not move the time: advance the timer first. A node whose time on the run's timer has not moved since its last update is skipped (it would see dt = 0): a step without an advance before it updates nothing, and a node given twice in one step updates once.

A node is not in this run.

RuntimeError

The run has stopped normally.

NetworkError

A node raised; the run has stopped.

docs.title: VirtualTimer
docs.text:
VirtualTimer()

Bases: Timer

A timer for tests: its time moves only when advance moves it.

It starts at 0. The scale is kept but does not apply to advance. mujou.testing.run runs a network on a new one (ManualRun.timer) unless given a timer; step the nodes by hand, so that every dt is exactly what the test advanced. Make one to share it between runs.

Example, with the node Error of the example of mujou.Run::

timer = VirtualTimer()
with mujou.testing.run(Error(), timer=timer) as run:
    timer.advance(0.001)
    run.step()  # every node updates once with dt = 0.001

docs.title: mujou.time
docs.text:
The time of mujou.

Every run measures its nodes' dt on one timer, a time axis that can be scaled and paused. By default every run shares the global timer, which the functions below read; give a run a Timer of its own with mujou.run(..., timer=...). Use these functions instead of the standard time module wherever a duration should follow the global time, e.g. to present an input for a while. The global time starts at 0 when the process first uses it.

  • now(): the global time as a Timestamp, as Timer.now gives a timer's (now().float() in seconds, now().ns in nanoseconds)
  • sleep(seconds): block for seconds of global time, following the scale and pauses
  • pause() / resume() / is_paused(): stop the global time and move it again, e.g. to take the states of several runs on it at one time
  • get_time_scale() / set_time_scale(scale): how many global seconds pass per real second (finite and > 0)
  • Timer: a time axis of its own for a run
  • ReadOnlyTimer: the reading side of a timer, as a node sees its run's timer (Node.timer)
  • Timestamp: a time on a timer, as Run.read_with_time and Port.recv_with_time give it

Only the host controls the time: sleep, set_time_scale, pause and resume raise RuntimeError in a node's hook.

docs.title: Timer
docs.text:
Timer()

A time axis that a run's nodes measure their dt on.

Timer() is a new time axis that starts at 0 on the real clock, at scale 1. Give it to mujou.run(..., timer=...) to run a network on a time of its own: a pause of that run (as Run.state_dict takes) then stops only this timer, not the global one that every other run uses by default. The nodes of the run read its time through Node.timer, a ReadOnlyTimer.

Times are Timestamp. Use sleep instead of the standard time.sleep wherever a duration should follow this time, e.g. to present an input to a run on this timer.

Only the host controls a timer: sleep, set_time_scale, pause and resume raise RuntimeError in a node's hook, where a node would wait for (or change the dt of) the other nodes.

pause stops the time of every run on the timer at one time T until resume. Take the states of several runs on one timer while it is paused, so that all of them are of the same time T: taken one after another on a running timer, each would be of a later time.

Example, with the node Error of the example of mujou.Run::

timer = mujou.time.Timer()
node = Error()
with mujou.run(node, timer=timer) as run:
    run.write({node.prev: torch.ones(2)})
    timer.sleep(0.1)  # 0.1 s of the run's time
    error, t = run.read_with_time(node.next)  # t is on this timer
    assert t <= timer.now()

pause() -> None

Stop the time of this timer until resume.

While paused, the time does not move: the nodes of the runs on this timer do not update (they wait until the time moves, and the first dt after resume does not count the pause), sleep does not return until resumed, and VirtualTimer.advance raises RuntimeError. Run.state_dict still works, so take the states of several runs on this timer at one time like this::

timer.pause()
try:
    trees = [run.state_dict() for run in runs]  # all at one time
finally:
    timer.resume()

ReadOnlyTimer(timer: Timer)

The reading side of a Timer: what a node sees of its run's timer as Node.timer.

ReadOnlyTimer(timer) takes the reading methods of timer (now and get_time_scale) and nothing else: it does not hold timer, so nothing reached from it sets the scale, advances the clock or waits on the time. A node thus cannot change the dt of the other nodes.

Once the host has seen a run end normally, each node's timer is replaced by a ReadOnlyTimer that stays at the time and the scale at which the run stopped, the time of the state. One that a node kept from before the end still reads the running timer.

Example::

class Clock(Node):  # sends the time of its run's timer, in seconds
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.next = NextPort(send=TensorSpec((), torch.float64))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        t = self.timer.now()  # a Timestamp on the run's timer
        self.next.send(torch.tensor(float(t), dtype=torch.float64))

docs.title: mujou.typing
docs.text:
Names for type annotations.

Write these in annotations only; the values that mujou works with are made by the names at the top level (Port, TensorSpec and so on).

  • Single: the peer count of a port that connects to at most one peer, the third type argument of Port[S, R, M] (the default of Port and PrevPort). recv() of such a port returns the message itself
  • Multi: the peer count of a port that connects to any number of peers (the default of NextPort, or multi=True). recv() of such a port returns a dict keyed by Channel
  • MessageSpec[T]: a spec of messages of type T. TensorSpec is a MessageSpec[torch.Tensor] and DictSpec(Sample, ...) a MessageSpec[Sample]. Annotate with it a function that takes either

An omitted direction is Never: PrevPort(recv=TensorSpec((3,))) is a PrevPort[Never, torch.Tensor, Single].

Example::

from typing import Never

import torch

from mujou import NextPort, PrevPort, TensorSpec
from mujou.typing import MessageSpec, Multi, Single


def sender[T](spec: MessageSpec[T]) -> NextPort[T, Never, Multi]:
    return NextPort(send=spec)


def mean_of(port: PrevPort[Never, torch.Tensor, Multi]) -> torch.Tensor:
    return torch.stack(list(port.recv().values())).mean(0)


inp: PrevPort[Never, torch.Tensor, Single] = PrevPort(recv=TensorSpec((3,)))

• quickstart.py: runs a two-node network with with mujou.run(...), writes input with write, and waits with run.wait_for(..., timeout=...) until the expected output arrives
  • leaky_chain/: a node defined in continuous time (a leaky integrator). The update uses the coefficient of the exact solution, so it is stable for any dt. The output is compared with the exact solution at the time elapsed from the write (the time that run.write returns) to the output
  • branching.py: sends from one NextPort to several nodes and merges them with PrevPort(multi=True). send_to sends only to the peer on a Channel that connect returned
  • group.py: Group(enc=..., dec=...) and mujou.run(a, b), and how node paths ("enc.scale", "0.scale") are named
  • save_and_restore.py: takes the state with run.state_dict(), saves it with torch.save (its tensors moved to the CPU), and restores it with mujou.run(..., state=...) to continue
  • pause.py: pauses the global timer with mujou.time.pause(), takes the states of two runs on it at that one time, and resumes it with mujou.time.resume(). A run restored from one of the states goes on from that time
  • subscribe.py: with run.subscribe, first receives the latest output at that moment, then the latest one each time a newer output is sent. If the next value is sent before one is received, the value in between is skipped. The loop stops with break after 20 values
  • online_learning.py: a teacher node sends a batch from y = a x + b every 10 ms, with the a that the host writes; the host changes a while the network runs. A learner learns once from each new batch, with no separate training and inference phases. The host follows the learner's loss with run.wait_for: it falls, jumps when the target changes, and falls again as the learner catches up
  • torch_node.py: trains an nn.Module inside a node with BP kept inside the node. Setting the seed, and an update that advances dt in smaller steps
  • testing_a_node.py: runs a node with a fixed dt and order, using the virtual timer and manual updates of mujou.testing, and compares the result bit for bit with a reference computation. It also checks that a run restored from a state taken midway matches a run that did not stop
  • timers.py: the time point Timestamp, the per-run timer Timer, and the speed of time (the run's timer and the global timer)
  • errors.py: the NetworkError the host receives and its __cause__, the order on_exception → on_stop, and that mujou.run raises an exception from on_start

Only leaky_chain/ is a directory. Its entry point is main.py, and the node definitions are in leaky.py.

docs.title: 🚀 Quickstart
docs.text:
Run the smallest program and read its output. The program connects two nodes to compute \(y = 2x + 1\).

flowchart LR
    H1["Host"] -->|"writes x"| S["scale (×2)"]
    S --> F["shift (+1)"]
    F -->|"reads y"| H2["Host"]

docs.title: The program
docs.text:
examples/quickstart.py
"""The smallest program: two nodes in a network, run in the background.

The host writes an input, follows the output until it arrives and stops.
"""

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((3,))  # every message here is a float32 vector of 3


class Scale(Node):
    """Sends its input times ``factor``."""

    def __init__(self, factor: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.factor = factor
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous side
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next side

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # the latest input; never waits
        self.next.send(self.factor * x)


class Shift(Node):
    """Sends its input plus ``offset``."""

    def __init__(self, offset: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.offset = offset
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.prev.recv() + self.offset)


class Affine(mujou.Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Scale(2.0)
        self.shift = Shift(1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev = self.scale.prev  # the input of the network
        self.next = self.shift.next  # the output of the network




net = Affine()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on threads of their own until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})  # the unconnected input port of scale
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
assert torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1)

Run it from the root of the repository.

uv run python examples/quickstart.py

It prints one line like this.

y = tensor([3., 5., 7.]) at t = 0.017 s

y is \(2x + 1\) for x = [1, 2, 3]. t is the time, in seconds of Mujou's global time, at which shift sent y. It changes from run to run.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
• Scale and Shift are nodes: classes that inherit from mujou.Node. Each declares its ports in __init__ and writes one step of work in on_update(dt). As in any subclass, they call super().__init__() and super().on_update(dt) first
  • Affine is a network: it holds the nodes as attributes, connects their ports with connect, and exposes the unconnected port prev of scale as its input and next of shift as its output
  • mujou.run(net) starts the nodes, each repeating on_update on a thread of its own, and returns once they are running. In on_update, recv() reads the latest value without waiting, so shift keeps sending values computed from older inputs (zeros at first) until x has passed through scale
  • So the output read right after run.write may still be old. run.write writes x, and run.wait_for waits until the output meets the condition, giving up with TimeoutError after 5 seconds of real time. Leaving the with block stops the network

docs.title: 🚩 Where to start
docs.text:
If you are new, read Writing a node, Building a network and Running a network, in that order. These three pages cover everything from writing your own node to running it.

The code examples on each page are taken from the programs in examples/, which the tests run.

docs.title: 🕸️ Building a Network
docs.text:
You write a network as a class that inherits from mujou.Network. This page shows how to:

  • connect nodes
  • expose ports to the outside
  • nest networks
  • branch and merge
  • check the built structure

How to think about networks is in Networks and Ports and channels.

docs.title: The basic form
docs.text:
In __init__, write these three things in order.

  1. Assign nodes (or other networks) to attributes
  2. Connect their ports with connect
  3. Expose the ports that should connect from outside, or that the host reads and writes, by assigning them to attributes of the network
class Affine(mujou.Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Scale(2.0)
        self.shift = Shift(1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev = self.scale.prev  # the input of the network
        self.next = self.shift.next  # the output of the network

Call super().__init__() first: the network registers each node, network and port as it is assigned to an attribute, as nn.Module registers submodules, and assigning one before super().__init__() raises AttributeError.

Assign each node to its own attribute

Nodes put in a list or a dict are not registered and do not become part of the network: assign each node to an attribute of its own.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Connect two ports with Port.connect, as in a.next.connect(b.prev). Nodes and networks have no connect of their own: a node can have several inputs and outputs, so naming the two ports always says which path you mean.

By convention, the port on the side of the previous node is a PrevPort named prev, and the port on the side of the next node is a NextPort named next, so a chain reads a.next.connect(b.prev).

The names and the kinds only make the direction readable. PrevPort and NextPort differ from Port only in how many peers they take by default (one for PrevPort, many for NextPort), and a node can have any number of each.

Two ports connect only when the send spec of one matches the recv spec of the other, in both directions. If they do not match, the call to connect raises TypeError. Connecting a second channel to a port that takes one peer raises ValueError.

connect returns the connection it made (a Channel). Use it to send a different value to each peer when branching (see Branching and merging below).

docs.title: Exposing ports
docs.text:
Assigning a child's port to an attribute of the network exposes that port. The kind of the port decides what the exposed port does.

The outside then names the port by a short name. By convention, a network exposes the port of its first node as prev and that of its last node as next (self.prev = self.l1.prev), so that it connects like a node: x.next.connect(net.prev) and net.next.connect(y.prev). Expose other ports under names of their own, such as net.teacher.

A network can expose only ports held by nodes inside it.

The host can write with run.write to any port that receives and is not connected, whether it is exposed or not. It names the port by following the attributes of the children, as in run.write({net.head.teacher: y}). Exposing a port only gives it a shorter name.

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
A network can hold another network as an attribute. If the child network exposes prev and next, connect them just like the ports of a node.

class Stack(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.l1 = Hidden(784, 256)
        self.l2 = Hidden(256, 256)
        self.l1.next.connect(self.l2.prev)
        self.prev = self.l1.prev
        self.next = self.l2.next


class Classifier(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.body = Stack()
        self.head = Head()
        self.body.next.connect(self.head.prev)  # body.next is l2.next itself
        self.prev = self.body.prev     # exposes again a port that the child exposed
        self.teacher = self.head.teacher

Hidden and Head are nodes that each have a PrevPort and a NextPort. Head also has a Port (teacher) that receives a teacher signal.

Nodes are told apart by their path: the attribute names from the root, joined with .. The paths of the nodes in this example are "body.l1", "body.l2" and "head".

Renaming an attribute changes the path

Renaming an attribute changes the path, and a state saved before the rename can no longer be restored (see Saving and restoring state).

A node cannot hold other nodes or networks as attributes: assigning one raises ValueError. To line up nodes, put them in attributes of a network.

docs.title: Branching and merging
docs.text:
Connecting several channels to one port makes a branch or a merge. The following example splits the output of split into two and joins them in sum.

class Split(Node):
    """Sends ``x`` on the channel ``plus`` and ``-x`` on the channel ``minus``."""

    # Channels of self.next, set by the network to the ones connect returned.
    plus: Channel
    minus: Channel

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)  # many peers by default

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()
        self.next.send_to(self.plus, x)
        self.next.send_to(self.minus, -x)


class Apply(Node):
    """Sends ``fn(x)``."""

    def __init__(self, fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fn = fn
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR, multi=False)  # exactly one peer here

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()
        self.next.send(self.fn(x))


class Sum(Node):
    """Sends the sum of the messages of all its peers."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR, multi=True)  # merges any number of peers
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        received = self.prev.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor]
        self.next.send(torch.stack(list(received.values())).sum(dim=0))


class Diamond(mujou.Network):
    """``split -> (double, square) -> sum``: y = 2 x + (-x)^2."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.split = Split()
        self.double = Apply(lambda x: 2 * x)
        self.square = Apply(lambda x: x**2)
        self.sum = Sum()
        # Hand split the channels it sends on: the order of connect does not matter.
        self.split.plus = self.split.next.connect(self.double.prev)
        self.split.minus = self.split.next.connect(self.square.prev)
        self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.square.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.prev = self.split.prev
        self.next = self.sum.next

docs.title: Branching: the sending side
docs.text:
A NextPort takes many peers by default, so writing a.next.connect(b.prev) and then a.next.connect(c.prev) makes a branch. There are two ways to send.

How to send Where it goes Value read by Run.read send(value) The same value to every peer Updated send_to(channel, value) Only to the peer at the end of channel Not updated

If the host reads with Run.read a port that only uses send_to, it gets the port's initial value (initial, or zeros). The host has no way to read the values sent with send_to themselves.

Run.read reads only ports that have a send type, so it cannot read the receive-only ports of the branches (each branch's prev) either. What the host can read is the result that a branch's node computed from the received value and sent with send (in the example above, 2 x at net.double.next).

Keep the Channel passed to send_to apart for each destination. As in the example above, the network assigns the Channel that connect returns to an attribute of the sending node (self.split.plus = self.split.next.connect(self.double.prev)).

Do not pick channels by their order

If the node takes them from self.next.channels (in the order of connection) instead, swapping the order of connect swaps the destinations without any error.

Attributes that hold a Channel are not collected into the state.

docs.title: Merging: the receiving side
docs.text:
PrevPort(multi=True) receives from many peers. On a port with many peers, recv() returns a dict keyed by Channel, in the order of connection. The value for the channel of a peer that has never sent is the initial value of the peer's port (zeros unless it declares initial).

The receiving node decides how to combine the values (sum them, average them, weight each peer, ...). Mujou does not combine them. Sum in the example above sums them.

To treat the peers differently, keep the Channel of each on the receiving node, as for send_to: self.sum.from_double = self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev), then self.prev.recv()[self.from_double] in the node.

A NextPort also takes many peers by default, so its recv() returns a dict. If the node is sure to have only one next node, declare NextPort(send=..., multi=False), and recv() returns the value itself.

docs.title: Checking the built structure
docs.text:
net.build() checks the structure and the types, freezes them, and returns the built structure (a Graph). mujou.run calls build() itself, so you need not call it just to run. Call it to check the structure before running.

net = Diamond()
graph = net.build()  # what mujou.run runs; mujou.run(net) builds the same graph
print("nodes:", [path for path, _ in graph.nodes])
print("output port:", graph.port_path(net.next))

build() freezes the network

After build():

  • no port in the tree can connect any more
  • no node, network or port can be assigned to or removed from the nodes and networks of the tree (both RuntimeError)
  • the network cannot become part of a bigger network

So call it only on the network you will run.

If the structure is invalid, build() raises ValueError with the reason. The API reference lists Graph and the causes.

docs.title: 🚨 Errors and Shutdown
docs.text: This page shows what happens when a hook of a node raises, and where the host receives the exception. It also covers the timeouts for waiting for the end and for taking the state.

docs.title: One node's exception stops everything
docs.text:
Whichever hook of whichever node raises (not only on_update, but also on_start, on_pause, state_dict and the rest), every node of the run stops. It goes as follows.

  1. Mujou catches the exception and logs the node's path, the hook's name and the traceback to the logger "mujou" at ERROR
  2. Each node finishes the hook it is running, stops, and calls its own on_exception() without waiting for the other nodes. Nodes that did not raise are called too
  3. Once on_exception() has finished on every node, on_stop() is called on every node. The node that raised is called too
  4. The host gets a NetworkError. Its __cause__ is the first exception. If several nodes raise at almost the same time, the exceptions after the first are only logged

Why everything stops

Mujou never stops only the node that raised and keeps the others running. Its neighbors would keep reading the stopped node's old values and drift away from the equilibrium without anyone noticing.

docs.title: Where the host receives it
docs.text:
The exception happens What raises NetworkError While starting (on_start and the like) mujou.run itself. It finishes the ending work (on_exception, on_stop) before it raises After the start The next write, read, subscribe (and its iterator), wait_for, state_dict, shutdown or join the host calls, or step of a ManualRun (mujou.testing.run)

An exception after the start does not reach the host until it next calls a method of Run.

Wait with run.join, not sleep

If the host waits without calling anything, it does not notice the exception. To wait until the run stops, use run.join(timeout), not mujou.time.sleep.

"""What happens when a node raises.

The whole run stops: every node's ``on_exception``, then its ``on_stop``, is
called, and the host gets a ``NetworkError`` whose ``__cause__`` is the node's
exception. An exception in ``on_start`` comes from ``mujou.run`` itself.
"""

import logging
import sys
from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NetworkError, NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

SCALAR = TensorSpec(())

# mujou also logs the node's exception, with its traceback, to the "mujou" logger.
# Show the log on stdout here (without a handler, Python prints it to stderr).
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="log: %(message)s")


class Checked(Node):
    """Passes its input on, and raises once it is negative."""

    def __init__(self, fail_on_start: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fail_on_start = fail_on_start
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=SCALAR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=SCALAR)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        if self.fail_on_start:
            raise RuntimeError("cannot start")

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        u = self.prev.recv()
        if u < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"negative input: {u.item()}")
        self.next.send(u)

    @override
    def on_exception(self) -> None:
        super().on_exception()
        print("on_exception: called on every node")

    @override
    def on_stop(self) -> None:
        super().on_stop()
        print("on_stop: called after on_exception")


class Single(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self, fail_on_start: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.checked = Checked(fail_on_start)
        self.prev = self.checked.prev


# An exception while the run goes on reaches the host at its next call.
net = Single()
run = mujou.run(net)
run.write({net.prev: torch.tensor(-1.0)})
try:
    run.join(timeout=10.0)  # waits until the run stops (here: by the exception)
except NetworkError as error:
    cause = error.__cause__
    print(f"NetworkError, caused by {type(cause).__name__}: {cause}")
    assert isinstance(cause, ValueError)

# An exception in on_start comes from mujou.run.
try:
    mujou.run(Single(fail_on_start=True))
except NetworkError as error:
    print(f"mujou.run raised NetworkError, caused by {error.__cause__!r}")
    assert isinstance(error.__cause__, RuntimeError)

NetworkError is a subclass of RuntimeError. To tell causes apart by type, look at error.__cause__.

docs.title: Inside a with statement
docs.text:
The with statement calls run.shutdown() when it exits.

  • If the body of the with finishes without an exception: the node's exception arrives at the end of the with statement, as the NetworkError raised by shutdown()
  • If the body of the with raises too: the body's exception propagates as it is, and the NetworkError is discarded. Check the node's exception in the log (see "Logging" below)

docs.title: on_exception and on_stop
docs.text:
Hook Called What to write on_exception() Only when the run ends with an exception. On every node, before on_stop Work specific to an abnormal end, such as a safe stop of actuators on_stop() Once at every end, normal or by an exception Release of resources such as I/O. Do not change the state
  • on_exception takes no arguments. A node cannot know which exception of which node stopped the run. The host handles the cause, by looking at __cause__
  • If you only want to handle an exception in your own hook, use try/except in that hook. An exception you catch does not stop the run
  • If on_exception or on_stop raises, the exception is only logged, and the ending goes on

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
A node's exception is logged with its traceback to the logger "mujou" at the ERROR level. In a program that has not configured logging, Python's default behavior prints it to standard error.

To send it elsewhere, configure Python's logging. The example above (examples/errors.py) sends it to standard output with the following lines.

# mujou also logs the node's exception, with its traceback, to the "mujou" logger.
# Show the log on stdout here (without a handler, Python prints it to stderr).
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="log: %(message)s")

docs.title: The state after an exception
docs.text:
The state of a run that ended with an exception is not saved. run.state_dict() raises NetworkError as well. To keep the state, take it regularly while the network runs (see Saving and restoring state).

To run again, create new instances, nodes included. A network can run only once.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
shutdown, join, subscribe and wait_for take an argument timeout in seconds of real time. The default is math.inf (wait forever).

Call When the time runs out run.shutdown(timeout) TimeoutError. The request to stop is not withdrawn, and the nodes update no more. The ending goes on in the background; wait for it with join run.join(timeout) TimeoutError. Nothing changes, and the run keeps running run.subscribe(port, timeout) TimeoutError from the iterator, at a step that begins after the time has run out or would wait past it. The time counts the whole iteration, the body of the loop included. The iterator ends, and the run keeps running run.wait_for(port, condition, timeout) TimeoutError. The run keeps running

run.state_dict(timeout) on a running network waits until every node has paused, at most timeout seconds of real time (30 by default). This timeout must be finite and greater than 0. After the run has ended there is nothing to wait for, and timeout is only checked.

If some node does not pause in time, run.state_dict() raises PauseTimeoutError (a subclass of TimeoutError). The message names the nodes that did not pause. No state is taken, the nodes that had paused resume too, and the run keeps running.

Long updates delay the pause

A state_dict timeout is likely with a node whose single on_update is long (heavy BP, for example), because a node finishes the running on_update before it pauses.

Passing a negative number or NaN as timeout raises ValueError; for state_dict, so do 0 and math.inf.

docs.title: Interpreter exit
docs.text:
If the interpreter exits while a run is running, Mujou stops the run and waits for on_stop on every node.

End each run yourself

Still, end each run yourself with shutdown() or a with statement.

docs.title: 🗂️ Grouping Networks
docs.text:
To run several networks in one run, pass them side by side as mujou.run(a, b), or combine them with mujou.Group.

This page shows how to write that, and when to split them into separate runs instead.

docs.title: How to write it
docs.text:
# By keyword: two networks connected before they are grouped.
enc, dec = Stage(2.0), Stage(3.0)
enc.next.connect(dec.prev)  # the ports a network exposes, as for nodes
x = torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0])
with mujou.run(Group(enc=enc, dec=dec), inputs={enc.prev: x}) as run:
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes, and how many fit in a given
    # time depends on how the threads get scheduled: follow the output until y
    # arrives (TimeoutError after 5 s).
    # The ports are those of the networks given.
    y, _ = run.wait_for(dec.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 6 * x), timeout=5.0)
    nodes = list(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
print(f"keyword: nodes {nodes}, y = {y}")
assert nodes == ["enc.scale", "dec.scale"]
assert torch.equal(y, 6 * x)

# By position: two independent networks in one run.
first, second = Stage(2.0), Stage(3.0)
with mujou.run(first, second, inputs={first.prev: x, second.prev: x}) as run:
    y1, _ = run.wait_for(first.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x), timeout=5.0)
    y2, _ = run.wait_for(second.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 3 * x), timeout=5.0)
    nodes = list(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
print(f"position: nodes {nodes}, y1 = {y1}, y2 = {y2}")
assert nodes == ["0.scale", "1.scale"]
assert torch.equal(y1, 2 * x) and torch.equal(y2, 3 * x)

mujou.run(a, b) is the same as mujou.run(Group(a, b)). To give names, use Group with keyword arguments.

The grouped networks have paths under the names given by Group.

Form Path of the node l1 in a mujou.run(a) "l1" mujou.run(a, b) "0.l1" Group(a, b) "0.l1" Group(enc=a, dec=b) "enc.l1"

The paths are the keys of the state tree. A position and a keyword give different paths.

Group the same way to restore

To restore a saved state, group the networks the same way as when the state was saved: the same order, and keywords only where they were used. Otherwise the paths do not match, and mujou.run(..., state=tree) raises ValueError (see Saving and restoring state).

mujou.run(node) with a single node adds no name either, like a single network. The path of the node is "", and the paths of its ports are "prev" and so on.

Group(node) adds a name, so there the path of the node is "0".

An invalid keyword (such as an empty name or one containing .) raises ValueError.

docs.title: Connect before grouping
docs.text:
Networks whose ports you connect with connect before grouping them run connected. Group itself connects nothing. The example above groups them with Group(enc=enc, dec=dec) after enc.next.connect(dec.prev).

To write input and read output, use the ports of the networks you passed as they are (enc.prev, dec.next). You do not have to go through the attributes of the Group.

A network built alone cannot be grouped later

If you run a network alone with mujou.run(a), that network is built alone. Passing the same network to mujou.run(a, b) afterwards raises RuntimeError, whether the first run is still running or has ended. Run them together from the start, or create new instances.

docs.title: Group them, or run them separately?
docs.text:
Grouped networks become one run. One run shares one timer, one state tree and one ending.

Decide whether to group or to split by whether you want to share these.

What is shared When grouped In separate runs, each given its own Timer Connecting Possible Not possible. Ports of another run cannot be connected Taking the state Pauses every node at once and takes the state at one time as one tree Taken per run. Taking it pauses only that run Time scale The same for every node Can differ per run Exceptions One node's exception ends every network Only the run of the node that raised ends

In the following cases, do not group them; use separate runs, and give each one a mujou.time.Timer().

  • You do not want to pause one when you take the state of the other
  • You want to speed up or slow down only one of them
  • You want one to keep running even if the other stops with an exception

Runs without a timer share the global timer

Even in separate runs, runs given no timer both share the global timer. Then taking the state of one stops the time of the other too. If they should not stop each other, give them separate Timers.

timer_a, timer_b = mujou.time.Timer(), mujou.time.Timer()
with mujou.run(a, timer=timer_a) as run_a, mujou.run(b, timer=timer_b) as run_b:
    timer_a.sleep(2.0)   # wait on the timer of a's run

How to use Timer is in Controlling time.

docs.title: 🏃 Running a Network
docs.text: mujou.run runs a network in the background and returns Run, the handle of the run. The host (the Python program that runs the network) writes input, reads output and ends the run with the methods of Run. This page shows how.

docs.title: The basic form
docs.text:
net = Affine()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on threads of their own until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})  # the unconnected input port of scale
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
  1. mujou.run(net) builds the network and starts every node. It returns after on_start (and load_state_dict on a restore) has finished on every node
  2. From then on, each node repeats on_update on its own thread, once every period. The host's thread does not stop
  3. The host writes input with write and reads output with read, read_with_time, subscribe or wait_for. The example above waits with wait_for until the expected value arrives
  4. When the with statement exits, shutdown() is called, and it waits until on_stop has finished on every node

mujou.run takes the following arguments.

Argument Meaning Default component, *components The networks or nodes to run. Two or more are combined into one run (see Composing networks) Required timer The run's timer (see Controlling time) None (the global timer) inputs The initial values of the input. {port: value} None state The state tree to restore (see Saving and restoring state) None

run.timer returns the run's timer: the timer you passed, or the global timer that mujou.time reads.

To run a single node, pass it as mujou.run(node) without wrapping it in a network. The path of the node is then "", and the paths of its ports are "prev" and so on (see Composing networks).

A network runs only once

Passing a network that was once passed to mujou.run to mujou.run again, whether it is still running or has ended, raises RuntimeError. To run again, create new instances, nodes included.

docs.title: Writing input
docs.text:
The host can write to a port that:

  • is unconnected
  • takes one peer
  • has a receive type

Nodes write to connected ports, so the host cannot write to them.

Way When to use it mujou.run(net, inputs={port: value}) Input to show from the first on_update (the initial value) run.write({port: value, ...}) To switch the input while the network runs

Without inputs, the initial value of the input is zeros.

Pass the first input with inputs

Once mujou.run returns, the nodes start repeating on_update right away. So if you write after mujou.run, the nodes may read zeros in the updates before the write. To show a non-zero input from the first update, pass it with inputs.

write behaves as follows.

  • A written value stays until the next write. Input is "a signal that changes over time", and nodes read the same input many times
  • The values of several ports written in one write switch at the same time. A node never reads the new value of only one of them. Put values that should switch as a pair, such as an input and its teacher signal, in one write
  • The values are copied. Changing the tensor after writing it does not reach the network
  • write returns the time the values were written

docs.title: Showing an input for a set time
docs.text:
Decide how long to show an input by waiting on the run's timer. If the run is on the global timer, use mujou.time.sleep(seconds).

Do not use time.sleep

Do not use the standard time.sleep, because it ignores changes of the time scale and the pauses for taking the state.

for x in stream:
    run.write({net.prev: x})
    mujou.time.sleep(0.1)          # show x for 0.1 seconds
    y = run.read(net.next)         # take the output at the end of showing as the response to x

The output catches up with a change of input after a delay. The network's dynamics (the time constants of the nodes, the number of stages) decide the length of the delay; Mujou does not. You choose a showing time long enough for the output to catch up.
