Reading right after write returns the output for the previous input. To match inputs with outputs, read at the end of the showing time. If you know the output to expect, wait for it with wait_for instead (see "Reading output" below).

docs.title: Reading output
docs.text:
There are four ways to read output.

Way What it returns Suited for run.read(port) The latest value at that moment The host reads whenever it suits it run.read_with_time(port) The latest value at that moment and the time it was sent, (value, Timestamp) Reading the value with its time run.subscribe(port) An iterator that yields (value, Timestamp) in turn Handling the output each time it is renewed run.wait_for(port, condition) The first (value, Timestamp) whose value meets condition Waiting until an expected output arrives

All of them read from any port that has a send type. All but read return the time as a mujou.time.Timestamp (see Controlling time).

Reading an unconnected port gives the network's output; reading a connected port observes the value of a node in the middle. The behavior of the nodes does not change.

read and read_with_time behave as follows.

  • It returns the value that the node holding the port last sent with send. If the node has not sent yet, it returns the port's initial value (initial, or zeros). Values sent with send_to are not reflected in read
  • The value is a new copy on the CPU

subscribe goes as follows.

  1. The first item is the latest value at the time of the call, returned without waiting. If nothing has been sent yet, it is the port's initial value
  2. After that, it waits until a new value is sent, and returns the latest value at that moment. If you read slowly, the values in between are skipped
  3. When the run ends normally, the iteration ends. When the run ends with a node's exception, the iteration raises NetworkError
  4. With timeout=seconds, the iteration raises TimeoutError once that many seconds of real time have passed since the call to subscribe, the time spent in the body of the loop included. The run keeps running. The default is forever

Only the host waits; the sending node does not wait for the host. The following example leaves the loop with break after 20 values. Without break or timeout, the loop blocks its thread until the run ends; another thread can end it by calling shutdown().

clock = Clock()  # a node runs by itself, without a network
with mujou.run(clock) as run:
    received: list[tuple[float, float]] = []
    # timeout: give up after 5 s of real time instead of waiting forever.
    for value, t in run.subscribe(clock.next, timeout=5.0):
        received.append((value.item(), float(t)))
        if len(received) == 20:
            break

To wait until an expected output arrives, use wait_for. It checks the latest value first, then each newer one, and returns the first that meets the condition. After timeout seconds of real time it raises TimeoutError (the run keeps running); if the run stops first, it raises RuntimeError.

y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, expected), timeout=5.0)

docs.title: Ending the run
docs.text:
Way What it does with mujou.run(...) as run: Calls shutdown() when the block exits. Use this normally run.shutdown(timeout=...) Asks every node to stop, and waits until on_stop has finished on every node run.join(timeout=...) Waits until the run ends, without asking it to stop. Use it after another thread calls shutdown(), or after shutdown times out

timeout is in seconds of real time, and the default is forever. What happens when it runs out is in "Timeouts" in Errors and shutdown.

Calling shutdown after a normal end does nothing. After a normal end, run.state_dict() still takes the last state (see Saving and restoring state). Calling write on a run that has ended raises RuntimeError.

Letting go of Run does not stop the run

Always end the run with shutdown or a with statement.

If any node raises, the whole network stops, and the later methods of Run raise NetworkError. Details are in Errors and shutdown.

docs.title: 💾 Saving and Restoring State
docs.text:
This page shows how to take the state of a running network, save it, and later run the network again from that state.

What the state tree holds, and how time stops while the state is taken, is in State.

docs.title: The basic steps
docs.text:
The following example runs a network for 0.2 seconds, takes its state, saves it with torch.save, restores it into a new instance, and goes on running.

"""Save the state of a run, and restore it in a new run that goes on from there.

A node collects its state by itself: every attribute that holds a
``torch.Tensor`` or an ``nn.Module``. ``Run.state_dict`` gathers the states of all
nodes, the latest messages and the time into one tree, a ``mujou.StateDict``.
Save it with ``torch.save`` (or pickle), and read it back with ``torch.load``.
"""

import io
from typing import override

import torch
from torch import nn

import mujou
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR1 = TensorSpec((1,))


class Integrator(Node):
    """Integrates its input over time (dx/dt = u) and sends ``readout(x)``."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR1)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR1)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        self.x = VECTOR1.zeros()  # a tensor: part of the state
        # A module: part of the state.
        self.readout = nn.Linear(1, 1, device=self.device)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.x += dt * self.prev.recv()  # in place, so that a restore copies into it
        self.next.send(self.readout(self.x))


class Model(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.integrator = Integrator()
        self.prev = self.integrator.prev
        self.next = self.integrator.next


one = torch.ones(1)

# Run for a while, then stop and take the state at the end.
net = Model()
with mujou.run(net, inputs={net.prev: one}) as run:
    mujou.time.sleep(0.2)
tree = run.state_dict()  # after a normal end: the state at the stop
saved = tree["nodes"]["integrator"]  # this node's state_dict()
print("state of the node:", {k: type(v).__name__ for k, v in saved.items()})
file = io.BytesIO()  # or a path, such as "state.pt"
# .cpu(): every tensor on the CPU, so that a machine without the GPU reads it too.
torch.save(tree.cpu(), file)

# A new instance of the same network goes on from the saved state and time.
restored = Model()
file.seek(0)
loaded = torch.load(file)  # the default weights_only=True reads a StateDict
with mujou.run(restored, inputs={restored.prev: one}, state=loaded) as run:
    mujou.time.sleep(0.1)
after = run.state_dict()["nodes"]["integrator"]

x0, x1 = saved["x"].item(), after["x"].item()
print(f"x = {x0:.3f} at the save, {x1:.3f} after 0.1 s more")
# The integral went on from the saved value: from 0, it would be about 0.1. (How
# far it gets in 0.2 s and 0.1 s depends on when the last update falls.)
assert x1 > x0 > 0
# The module was restored too: the new instance had other random weights.
assert torch.equal(after["readout"]["weight"], saved["readout"]["weight"])

The steps are as follows.

  1. The node keeps the values of its state in attributes that hold a torch.Tensor or an nn.Module. mujou.Node collects them into the state automatically (self.x and self.readout in the example)
  2. The node creates the state tensors in on_start, and updates them in place in on_update (+=, add_, copy_, ...)
  3. The host takes the state tree with run.state_dict(). It works while the network runs, and also after the with statement exits (after a normal end)
  4. The host saves the tree with torch.save or the like. How to save it is up to the host
  5. To restore, create a new instance of the same network and pass it as mujou.run(net, state=tree)

Step 2 updates in place because the default load_state_dict restores the state by copying into the tensors created in on_start. With in-place updates, any other attribute or local variable that refers to the same tensor also sees the restored values.

Step 5 needs a new instance because a network can run only once. Passing the network the tree was taken from to mujou.run again raises RuntimeError.

docs.title: When you restore
docs.text:
• The timer goes back to the time of the tree. On the default global timer, restoring sets the global time (mujou.time.now()) back to the time the tree was taken. When mujou.run(..., state=tree) returns, the time has already gone back. Do not compare a mujou.time.now() read before the restore with a time read after it. Measure elapsed time as the difference between two times read after the restore
  • You cannot restore while another run is running on the same timer. In that case mujou.run raises ValueError and starts nothing. End the other run first, or give the restored run a timer of its own, mujou.time.Timer() (see Controlling time)
  • The restored network must have the same node paths and connections as the network the tree was taken from. Otherwise mujou.run raises ValueError
  • If you pass both state= and inputs=, the values in inputs override the input values in the tree

docs.title: Taking the states of several runs at one time
docs.text:
run.state_dict() takes the state of one run at one time. When several runs share a timer (by default, all of them run on the global timer) and you take their states one after another, each state is of a later time than the one before, because the time goes on in between.

To take them all at one time, pause the timer first, take the states, and resume it.

# Two runs on the global timer, such as two agents that should be saved together.
a, b = Clock(), Clock()
with mujou.run(a) as run_a, mujou.run(b) as run_b:
    mujou.time.sleep(0.1)
    mujou.time.pause()  # the global time stops at one time T
    try:
        tree_a = run_a.state_dict()  # still works while paused
        tree_b = run_b.state_dict()
    finally:
        mujou.time.resume()  # the time goes on from T
    mujou.time.sleep(0.05)

# Both trees are of T, and no update in them is later than T.
t_ns = tree_a["timer"]["time_ns"]
assert tree_b["timer"]["time_ns"] == t_ns
assert tree_a["last_update_ns"][""] <= t_ns and tree_b["last_update_ns"][""] <= t_ns
data = pickle.dumps({"a": tree_a, "b": tree_b})  # save them together

run.state_dict() works while the timer is paused, and every tree then holds the time of the pause. While paused, the nodes do not update, and the paused time does not enter the dt after resume (see Pausing the time).

Put resume in finally

Put the resume in finally, so that an exception does not leave the time stopped.

To restore the trees, note that a run cannot restore while another run is running on the same timer. Restore them one after another once the previous run has ended, or give each restored run a timer of its own; each timer then starts from the same time of the trees.

docs.title: The state is not saved after an exception
docs.text:
When a run ends with an exception, run.state_dict() raises NetworkError and returns no state (see Errors and shutdown).

Save regularly during a long run

If you do not want to lose the state of a long run, take run.state_dict() regularly while it runs and save it.

docs.title: Putting other values in the state
docs.text:
Only torch.Tensor and nn.Module values assigned directly to attributes are collected (see How Mujou works). The following are not collected.

  • Number attributes (such as a step counter)
  • Lists and dicts of tensors
  • The state of the random number generator self.generator
  • The state of an optimizer (such as moments) and the gradients accumulated in .grad

To put these in the state, override both state_dict and load_state_dict. Call super(), and the automatically collected part is handled as before.

For a number, you can instead keep it as a 0-dimensional tensor created in on_start (self.count = torch.zeros((), device=self.device)) and update it in place (self.count += 1), without overriding anything. It is then collected automatically.

The following example adds the state of the random number generator. The generator is created again from seed every time the run starts. Without its state, the random numbers after a restore differ from those of a run that went on without stopping.

from typing import Any, override

from mujou import Node


class Noisy(Node):
    @override
    def state_dict(self) -> Any:
        state = super().state_dict()
        state["generator"] = self.generator.get_state()
        return state

    @override
    def load_state_dict(self, state: Any) -> None:
        state = dict(state)  # copy first, so the given tree is not modified
        self.generator.set_state(state.pop("generator"))
        super().load_state_dict(state)

When you override them, follow these rules.

Hook Rules state_dict() Return an object that pickles. Do not call recv or send on a port in it (that raises RuntimeError). You may put the live tensors in it; Mujou copies the tree load_state_dict(state) state is a copy of what state_dict() returned. It is called on the node's thread, after on_start and before the first on_update

Do not change the state in on_stop

Do not change the state in on_stop. After a normal end, run.state_dict() copies the state as the nodes left it, after on_stop, with the time at which shutdown asked the run to stop. A change made in on_stop would go into the tree (the reason is in State).

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
The tree run.state_dict() returns is a mujou.StateDict. It is a subclass of dict: you index it as a dict, and you can save it with pickle or with torch.save. A tree read back is a mujou.StateDict again.

For your own files, either will do. To share a tree with others, save it with torch.save, so that they can read it with the default torch.load. mujou.run(..., state=) takes a mujou.StateDict, or a plain dict of the same items.

Read a file back the same way it was saved (pickle.loads for pickle.dumps, torch.load for torch.save). If you do not know how a file was saved, read it first with the default torch.load. If that fails, read it with pickle only when you trust the sender.

  • torch.load with its default (weights_only=True) reads a tree made only of tensors, numbers, strings, dicts, lists and tuples. It reads a mujou.StateDict too, once mujou is imported. If you override state_dict to put objects of your own classes in the tree, the default torch.load cannot read it
  • pickle.load and torch.load(..., weights_only=False) can run code from the file while reading it. Do not read files you do not trust with them
  • The state of a node that computes on CUDA goes into the tree as CUDA tensors. tree.cpu() returns a new tree with every tensor of the tree on the CPU (the tree itself is not changed). Move the tree to the CPU before saving it, and a machine without a GPU can read it too. To read a file saved with CUDA tensors, use torch.load(..., map_location="cpu"). The default load_state_dict copies to the node's device, so you can pass the CPU tensors to state= as they are
torch.save(run.state_dict().cpu(), "state.pt")  # the state of GPU nodes as CPU tensors
tree = torch.load("state.pt")  # a mujou.StateDict

tree.to(device) moves every tensor of the tree to device, and cpu() is to("cpu").

It looks into the dicts (including the OrderedDict of the state_dict of an nn.Module), lists and tuples of the tree, and makes these containers anew. Other values are shared with the original tree. As with torch.Tensor.to, a tensor already on device is not copied but shared with the original tree

docs.title: 🧪 Testing
docs.text:
In a network run the usual way, dt follows the real time that passes, and the order in which the nodes update differs every time. So the results differ slightly from run to run.

This page shows how to use mujou.testing to run nodes and networks with the same result every time, and test them. Mujou's own tests use the same API.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Import mujou.testing with import mujou.testing. import mujou alone does not import it.

Name Role mujou.testing.run(net, ...) Runs the network with the same arguments as mujou.run and returns a ManualRun. No node updates until step lets it. The run is on a new VirtualTimer unless you pass a timer mujou.testing.VirtualTimer() A virtual timer. It starts at time 0 and moves only by what you pass to advance(seconds) ManualRun.timer The timer of the run: the VirtualTimer that mujou.testing.run made, or the timer you passed ManualRun.step(*nodes) Updates the given nodes once each, in the given order, and returns when all are done

ManualRun is a subclass of Run, so write, read, state_dict and the rest work as they do with mujou.run.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The following test compares a network of two leaky integrators in a row with a discrete algorithm written with the same exact coefficient as the nodes, 1 - exp(-h / tau).

"""Test a node deterministically with ``mujou.testing``.

``mujou.testing.run`` runs on a ``VirtualTimer``, whose time moves only when the
test advances it, and ``ManualRun.step`` updates the nodes by hand in a fixed order.
Every ``dt`` is then exactly the step, and the run can be compared with the discrete
algorithm, or with a run restored from a state taken midway.
"""

import math
from typing import Any, override

import torch

import mujou
import mujou.testing
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((2,), torch.float64)


class Leaky(Node):
    """dx/dt = (u - x) / tau, exact for an input held constant over each ``dt``."""

    def __init__(self, tau: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.tau = tau
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        self.x = VECTOR.zeros()

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.x += (1 - math.exp(-dt / self.tau)) * (self.prev.recv() - self.x)
        self.next.send(self.x)


class Chain(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self, tau: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a = Leaky(tau)
        self.b = Leaky(tau)
        self.a.next.connect(self.b.prev)
        self.prev = self.a.prev
        self.next = self.b.next


def test_chain_follows_the_discrete_algorithm() -> None:
    tau, h, steps = 0.01, 0.001, 50
    u = torch.tensor([1.0, -2.0], dtype=torch.float64)

    # The reference: the discrete algorithm, a then b at every step.
    a, b = VECTOR.zeros(), VECTOR.zeros()
    for _ in range(steps):
        a += (1 - math.exp(-h / tau)) * (u - a)
        b += (1 - math.exp(-h / tau)) * (a - b)  # b reads the new a

    net = Chain(tau)
    # On a new VirtualTimer at time 0 (run.timer), which moves only by advance.
    with mujou.testing.run(net, inputs={net.prev: u}) as run:
        for _ in range(steps):
            run.timer.advance(h)  # every node's next dt is exactly h
            run.step(net.a, net.b)  # a, then b, which reads a's new value
        y, t = run.read_with_time(net.next)

    assert torch.equal(y, b)  # the same operations: equal to the last bit
    assert t.ns == steps * 1_000_000  # sent at the time of the last step
    print(f"after {steps} steps of {h} s: y = {y}, equal to the reference")
  1. Write the reference with the same operations as the nodes. Here it updates a, then updates b with the new value of a
  2. Run the network with mujou.testing.run(net, inputs=...). It runs on a new VirtualTimer at time 0, which run.timer returns
  3. At each step, first move the time h seconds forward with run.timer.advance(h), then update the nodes with run.step(...). The dt of each node is then exactly h
  4. Read the output with run.read and compare it with the reference

Comparing with the reference

If the reference and the nodes do the same operations in the same order, the results match to the last bit, so you can compare them with torch.equal. If the order of operations differs, compare with torch.testing.assert_close.

docs.title: Rules of step
docs.text:
• step() with no arguments updates every node once, in the order of the network's tree
  • The order changes the result. With step(net.a, net.b) in the example above, b reads the value a sent in this step. With step(net.b, net.a), b reads the value of a from the previous step
  • A node whose timer has not moved since its last update is skipped (it would see dt = 0). If you forget advance, nothing happens, and if you pass the same node twice in one step, the second one is skipped
  • The period of a node (period) is not used in a manual run
  • step does not move the time. Only advance moves it

Do not wait without a timeout on the stepping thread

Nothing is sent unless step is called. So wait_for and subscribe without a timeout on the thread that calls step wait forever.

docs.title: Choosing the timer
docs.text:
By default, mujou.testing.run makes a new VirtualTimer for each run, unlike mujou.run, whose default is the global timer. Pass a timer in these cases.

  • To run several runs on one time axis, for example to restore a state on the timer of the run that took it (see "Testing save and restore" below), create a VirtualTimer() and pass the same one to each run
  • To pass a Timer that is not virtual. Its clock then moves by itself, and each dt is the real time that passed between steps. Such a test is not deterministic

docs.title: Other conditions for determinism
docs.text:
• Give a seed to nodes that use random numbers (see PyTorch in nodes). Without a seed, the generator is made with a different seed every time
  • In tests too, the host does not wait with time.sleep to decide a result. Move the time with advance

docs.title: Testing save and restore
docs.text:
You can check that a run that takes the state midway and continues in a new instance matches a run that went on without stopping. On a VirtualTimer, the two match to the last bit.

The following test continues the program above. The second half restores onto the same timer as the first half; this is allowed because the first half has already ended.

def run_steps(
    net: Chain,
    timer: mujou.testing.VirtualTimer,
    n: int,
    state: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Run ``net`` for ``n`` steps of 1 ms on ``timer`` and return its state."""
    u = torch.tensor([1.0, -2.0], dtype=torch.float64)
    with mujou.testing.run(net, timer=timer, inputs={net.prev: u}, state=state) as run:
        for _ in range(n):
            timer.advance(0.001)
            run.step()
    return run.state_dict()


def test_restored_run_matches_a_straight_run() -> None:
    straight = run_steps(Chain(0.01), mujou.testing.VirtualTimer(), 20)
    # Ten steps, then ten more in a new instance restored from the first half. The
    # second half runs on the timer of the first, which has ended.
    timer = mujou.testing.VirtualTimer()
    half = run_steps(Chain(0.01), timer, 10)
    resumed = run_steps(Chain(0.01), timer, 10, state=half)

    assert torch.equal(resumed["nodes"]["b"]["x"], straight["nodes"]["b"]["x"])
    print("save and restore: equal to the run that did not stop")

docs.title: Testing exceptions
docs.text:
When a node raises, the exception reaches you from step as a NetworkError. Its __cause__ is the node's exception (see Errors and shutdown).

After that, every call of the run raises it again, including the shutdown at the end of the with block, so put pytest.raises around the whole block, in the same with statement:

import pytest

import mujou.testing
from mujou import NetworkError

with pytest.raises(NetworkError) as info, mujou.testing.run(net) as run:
    run.timer.advance(0.001)
    run.step()  # a node raises ValueError here
assert isinstance(info.value.__cause__, ValueError)

docs.title: ⏱️ Controlling Time
docs.text:
This page shows how to read the time, wait on it, change how fast it runs, and give a run its own timer.

Why a node updates in proportion to dt, and why a pause does not make time jump, is in Global time.

docs.title: What to use where
docs.text:
To Host (default global timer) Host (run on a Timer of its own) In a node's hook Read the time mujou.time.now() (a Timestamp) timer.now() self.timer.now() Wait on the time mujou.time.sleep(seconds) timer.sleep(seconds) Not allowed Read the time scale mujou.time.get_time_scale() timer.get_time_scale() self.timer.get_time_scale() Change the time scale mujou.time.set_time_scale(scale) timer.set_time_scale(scale) Not allowed Stop and restart time mujou.time.pause() / mujou.time.resume() timer.pause() / timer.resume() Not allowed See whether time stopped mujou.time.is_paused() timer.is_paused() Not available

Do not wait with time.sleep

The host waits with the sleep of the run's timer (to show an input for a certain time, for example), not with the standard time.sleep of Python. The standard time.sleep waits in real time: it ignores the time scale, and it goes on counting while the run pauses (a run pauses while its state is taken).

The scale is how many seconds of the timer pass per real second (at 5, one real second is 5 seconds of the timer). It is a finite number greater than 0. Anything else raises ValueError.

docs.title: Timestamp
docs.text:
The times that run.write, run.read_with_time, run.subscribe and run.wait_for return, and the values of mujou.time.now(), timer.now() and self.timer.now(), are all mujou.time.Timestamp.

Form Value ts.float() Seconds (float). float(ts) is the same ts.ns Nanoseconds (int). The exact value later - earlier The seconds from earlier to later (float). Negative if later is earlier a < b and so on Which time is earlier

Compare only times from the same timer

A Timestamp does not record which timer it is from. Compare only times from the same timer. Compare with mujou.time.now() only the times of a run on the global timer.

Comparing the time that write returns with the time that read_with_time returns tells whether an output was sent after the input was switched.

t_in = run.write({net.prev: x})
mujou.time.sleep(0.1)
y, t_out = run.read_with_time(net.next)
if t_out >= t_in:               # y was sent after x was written
    print(t_out - t_in)  # seconds from writing x until y was sent

docs.title: A timer for one run
docs.text:
Create mujou.time.Timer() and pass it as mujou.run(..., timer=timer), and the run runs on that timer. A new timer starts at time 0 with scale 1.

# A run on a timer of its own, ten times faster than the real time. Pausing this
# run (to take its state, say) stops only this timer, not the global one.
timer = Timer()  # starts at 0
timer.set_time_scale(10.0)
clock = Clock()
start_real, start_global = time.perf_counter(), mujou.time.now()
with mujou.run(clock, timer=timer) as run:
    timer.sleep(2.0)  # 2 s of the run's time: about 0.2 s of real time
    # The clock sends once per update, and when it updates depends on how the
    # threads get scheduled: wait until it has sent a time from 2 s on. The timeout
    # is in real seconds, whatever the timer's scale.
    seen, t = run.wait_for(clock.next, lambda now: now.item() >= 2.0, timeout=5.0)
elapsed_real = time.perf_counter() - start_real
elapsed_global = mujou.time.now() - start_global
print(
    f"run's time {float(t):.2f} s, real {elapsed_real:.2f} s, "
    f"global {elapsed_global:.2f} s"
)
# The run's 2 s took less real time (about 0.2 s, but a busy machine takes longer).
assert float(t) >= 2.0 and elapsed_real < 2.0
# The clock read its time just before it sent: compare times of the same timer
# only, since a Timestamp does not say which timer it is on.
assert seen.item() <= float(t)

Give a run its own timer in these cases.

  • You want to speed up or slow down only that run (for debugging, or for trials faster than real time)
  • You want to restore a state while another run is running on the global timer (see Saving and restoring state)
  • You run several networks in separate runs that should not stop each other (see Grouping networks)

The host then waits on that run with timer.sleep, and compares the times from run.read_with_time with timer.now(). run.timer returns the timer of a run, the global timer if you passed none.

Do not use the functions of mujou.time for this run

The functions of mujou.time (mujou.time.sleep, mujou.time.now(), ...) work on the global timer, not on this run's timer, so do not use them for this run.

docs.title: Changing the speed of the global timer
docs.text:
mujou.time.set_time_scale changes the speed of every run on the global timer.

# The global timer can be scaled too; it then applies to every run on it.
mujou.time.set_time_scale(5.0)
start_real = time.perf_counter()
mujou.time.sleep(0.5)  # 0.5 s of the global time: about 0.1 s of real time
print(f"slept 0.5 s of global time in {time.perf_counter() - start_real:.2f} s real")
mujou.time.set_time_scale(1.0)

The global time starts at 0 when the process first uses it.

docs.title: Pausing the time
docs.text:
timer.pause() stops the time of the timer until timer.resume(); mujou.time.pause() and mujou.time.resume() do the same for the global timer.

Use it when the host does something that should happen at one time, such as taking the states of several runs on the same timer (see Saving and restoring state).

While the time is paused:

  • The nodes of every run on the timer do not update. They wait until the time moves again, and the first dt after resume does not count the pause
  • sleep on the timer does not return until the time moves again
  • VirtualTimer.advance raises RuntimeError
  • run.state_dict() still works, and gives the state at the time of the pause

pause is a switch, not a count

pause is a switch, not a count: calling it twice still needs only one resume. Taking the state pauses the timer too, apart from this switch, so resume does not cut that short, and the end of taking the state does not end your pause. is_paused() is true while either one stops the time.

docs.title: Nodes only read the time
docs.text:
A node's self.timer is the read-only side of the run's timer (mujou.time.ReadOnlyTimer). It has only now() and get_time_scale().

Calling sleep, set_time_scale, pause or resume of mujou.time or of a Timer, or VirtualTimer.advance, in a hook raises RuntimeError. If one node stopped the time or changed its speed, it would change the dt of the other nodes in the same run too.

  • To update a node at regular intervals, do not wait in a hook. Pass a period with super().__init__(period=seconds). The period is the average time between two updates, in seconds of the run's timer (see Writing a node)
  • self.timer can be read in every hook, on_thread_start and on_start included. Reading it in __init__ raises RuntimeError

docs.title: Restoring sets the time back
docs.text: Restoring with mujou.run(..., state=tree) sets the run's timer back to the time the tree was taken. On the global timer, mujou.time.now() goes back too. Details are in Saving and restoring state.

docs.title: Use a virtual timer in tests
docs.text: To give dt a fixed value in a test, use mujou.testing.VirtualTimer. The steps are in Testing.

docs.title: 🔥 PyTorch in Nodes
docs.text: A node computes with PyTorch inside. This page covers update rules, devices and random numbers, backpropagation (BP) inside a node, CUDA, and the settings that affect the whole process.

docs.title: Update rules
docs.text:
The update a node writes in on_update(dt) is that node's update rule (its learning rule). Mujou builds no update rule into nodes, ports or the execution machinery, so each node chooses its own and can swap it.

  • The default update rule is PC-ALM (Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding, https://pub.sakana.ai/pc-alm/). It is reported to perform close to BP with local updates. The choice is provisional
  • BP is also an update rule, as long as it stays inside one node (see "BP inside a node" below)

The PC-ALM nodes are not implemented yet

The PC-ALM nodes are planned for the module mujou.pc, which is not implemented yet. Until then, subclass mujou.Node and write the update equations yourself in on_update(dt) (see Writing a node).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The following node learns a linear map from its input to the target online, and sends its prediction. BP stays inside the one node.

BATCH, N_IN, N_OUT = 16, 4, 2
INPUT, OUTPUT = TensorSpec((BATCH, N_IN)), TensorSpec((BATCH, N_OUT))
MAX_STEP = 0.01  # seconds: a longer explicit Euler step could diverge


class Regressor(Node):
    """Learns to map its input to the target online, and sends its prediction."""

    def __init__(self, rate: float) -> None:
        super().__init__(seed=0)  # the seed of self.generator; computes on the CPU
        self.rate = rate
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=INPUT)
        self.target = Port(recv=OUTPUT)
        self.next = NextPort(send=OUTPUT)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        self.model = nn.Linear(N_IN, N_OUT, device=self.device)
        # The node's own generator, not the global one that all nodes share.
        nn.init.normal_(self.model.weight, std=0.1, generator=self.generator)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.model.bias)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x, y = self.prev.recv(), self.target.recv()
        params = list(self.model.parameters())
        # Split a long dt into n equal steps instead of clipping it: none of the
        # elapsed time is lost.
        n = max(1, math.ceil(dt / MAX_STEP))
        h = dt / n
        for _ in range(n):
            with torch.enable_grad():  # mujou: local-autograd
                loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(self.model(x), y)
                grads = torch.autograd.grad(loss, params)
            for p, g in zip(params, grads, strict=True):
                p -= h * self.rate * g  # in place, outside the block: not recorded
        self.next.send(self.model(x))

In online_learning.py in Examples, a node like this learns from a stream whose target changes partway through the run, and keeps up with the change.

docs.title: Device and seed
docs.text:
Pass the device and the random seed in __init__, with super().__init__(device=..., seed=...).

  • device is the CPU (the default, "cpu") or a CUDA device. Mujou supports only these two. Any other device, such as "mps" or "meta", raises ValueError, and so does a CUDA device when CUDA is not available
  • Received messages (the values of recv()) arrive on the node's device
  • Allocate tensors with device=self.device

docs.title: Random number generator
docs.text:
Draw random numbers from the node's own generator, self.generator. The generator is made from seed and lives on the node's device.

nn.init.normal_(self.model.weight, std=0.1, generator=self.generator)
noise = torch.randn(4, generator=self.generator, device=self.device)
  • self.generator is created on the node's thread, so you can use it from on_start on. Using it in __init__ raises RuntimeError
  • Do not call torch.manual_seed in a node. The default generator is shared by the whole process, so it would change the random numbers of other nodes too
  • The generator is created again from seed every time the run starts. To continue the same random sequence after a restore, put the generator's state in the state tree (see Saving and restoring state)

docs.title: BP inside a node
docs.text:
Mujou turns gradient recording off on every node's thread (torch.set_grad_enabled(False)). The default update rule, PC-ALM, computes its update equations directly, so it will need no autograd graph.

To use autograd in a node, write it as follows.

  1. Wrap both the forward pass and the gradient computation (torch.autograd.grad or .backward()) in with torch.enable_grad():
  2. Mark that with line with # mujou: local-autograd. The mark says that BP stays inside this node
  3. Update the parameters in place, outside the block (p -= h * self.rate * g in the example). No gradient is recorded outside the block, so the update does not enter the autograd graph

BP stays inside the node. A node cannot pass gradients to another node: recv() returns a copy, and send() detaches the value with detach() before sending it.

  • Do not use torch.inference_mode(). Tensors created in it cannot be used for backward
  • Gradients accumulated in .grad by .backward(), and the state of an optimizer, are not put in the state tree automatically. To continue the same way after a restore, override state_dict to add them (see Saving and restoring state)
  • Make the update size proportional to dt. The example splits dt into n steps h = dt / n, each no longer than MAX_STEP. It computes the gradient again for each step and updates n times. Explicit Euler then does not diverge when dt is long, and no elapsed time is lost

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
For a node given a CUDA device, Mujou sets up the following.

  • It makes the node's device the current device of the node's thread
  • It creates a CUDA stream for the node alone and makes it the current stream of that thread. All of the node's operations go on this stream
  • It synchronizes the node's stream after each on_update, and around taking and restoring the state

So the node's author does not have to write any synchronization. If you synchronize yourself, synchronize only your own stream (torch.cuda.current_stream().synchronize()).

Do not wait for the whole device

Do not use torch.cuda.synchronize(), which waits for the whole device, including the work of other nodes.

Without an index, as in device="cuda", the device is the host's current device at the time the node is created.

In the tree run.state_dict() returns, the state of a CUDA node stays in CUDA tensors. Move every tensor of the tree to the CPU with cpu() before saving it, and a machine without a GPU can read it too. On a restore, the default load_state_dict copies the tensors back to the node's device (see Saving and restoring state).

torch.save(run.state_dict().cpu(), "state.pt")

docs.title: Settings of the whole process
docs.text:
The following settings are shared by the whole process. Do not change them in a node. If needed, the host sets them once, before mujou.run.

  • torch.manual_seed and the default random number generator
  • torch.set_num_threads, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms, and the flags in torch.backends.*
  • Operations on a whole device, such as torch.cuda.synchronize() and torch.cuda.empty_cache()

A node may change only per-thread settings. Write them in on_thread_start, a hook called once on the node's thread just before on_start.

docs.title: Internal threads
docs.text:
Each node computes on its own thread. On the CPU, torch operations use further internal threads for each of those threads. With too many internal threads, the nodes compete for the CPU and everything slows down.

Mujou does not set the number of internal threads, so the host decides it before mujou.run.

# Each node computes on its own thread, and torch adds threads of its own for
# each: keep those few (a setting of the whole process, made by the host).
torch.set_num_threads(1)

Rule of thumb for the number of threads

The number of nodes that compute on the CPU times the n of torch.set_num_threads(n) should not exceed the number of physical cores. With many nodes on small matrices, n = 1 is enough.

docs.title: 🧩 Writing a Node
docs.text: You write a node as a class that inherits from mujou.Node. This page shows how, step by step. For what a node is, see How Mujou works.

docs.title: Example: a leaky integrator
docs.text:
This node follows its input \(u\) with the time constant \(\tau\). Its state \(x\) follows \(\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{u - x}{\tau}\).

"""A leaky integrator: a node whose dynamics is defined in continuous time."""

import math
from typing import override

import torch

from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

SCALAR = TensorSpec((), torch.float64)


class Leaky(Node):
    """Follows its input ``u`` with the time constant ``tau`` (in seconds):

        dx/dt = (u - x) / tau

    ``on_update`` advances ``x`` by ``dt``, the time that passed since the last
    update, with the exact solution for an input held constant over the step:
    ``x`` moves the fraction ``1 - exp(-dt / tau)`` of the way to ``u``. That
    fraction stays below 1 for any ``dt``, so a long ``dt`` (a busy machine) never
    overshoots ``u``, and none of the elapsed time is lost.

    ``period`` is well below ``tau`` by default: a node downstream sees this
    output at most about one period late, a small delay next to ``tau``.
    """

    def __init__(self, tau: float, period: float = 0.001) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=period)
        self.tau = tau
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=SCALAR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=SCALAR)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        self.x = SCALAR.zeros()  # the state: collected by the node automatically

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        u = self.prev.recv()
        self.x += (1 - math.exp(-dt / self.tau)) * (u - self.x)  # in place
        self.next.send(self.x)

The node writes three things.

  1. In __init__, it declares the ports (prev and next)
  2. In on_start, it sets up the state x
  3. In on_update(dt), it reads the input, updates the state in proportion to dt, and sends the result

The sections below follow this order.

Always call super() first

As in any subclass, __init__ first calls super().__init__(), and each overridden hook first calls the same hook of super(). The hooks of mujou.Node do nothing, except state_dict and load_state_dict (see State).

Call them anyway: then your node keeps working when it later inherits from a node class of your own whose hooks do something.

docs.title: 1. Declare the ports in __init__
docs.text:
Assign ports as instance attributes inside __init__, after super().__init__().

  • Before super().__init__(): the node registers each port as it is assigned, and assigning one before super().__init__() raises AttributeError
  • As a class attribute: a port declared as a class attribute makes building the network (build()) raise ValueError

Choose the kind of port by its role in the network. By convention, name the port on the side of the previous node prev and the one on the side of the next node next, so that a chain reads a.next.connect(b.prev).

Role Declaration Name by convention The side that receives from the previous node PrevPort prev The side that sends to the next node NextPort next Anything else (a teacher signal input, an output for observation, ...) Port any

The kinds differ only in the number of peers they take by default (below). A node can have any number of ports of each kind.

Give each port the type of the values it sends as send=, and the type of the values it receives as recv=. Write a type as TensorSpec(shape, dtype).

If you leave out the dtype, it is torch.get_default_dtype() at the time the spec is created (usually float32). On a one-way port, leave out the argument you do not use (do not pass None).

self.prev = PrevPort(recv=TensorSpec((32, 784)))                       # receive only
self.next = NextPort(send=TensorSpec((32, 256)), recv=TensorSpec((32, 256)))  # both ways

multi= decides the number of peers. By default, PrevPort and Port take one peer and NextPort takes many. On a port with many peers, recv() returns a dict, not the value itself (see Branching and merging in Building a network).

A value you send must match the spec in both shape and dtype. The dtype is not converted automatically. The Leaky above uses a torch.float64 spec, so it also creates the values it sends as float64.

Until a port first sends, its peers receive zeros, and so does the host that reads it. To start from another value, give the port an initial value with initial=. It must match send in shape and dtype, and it is copied when the port is made.

A restored run (see State) starts from the values in the state instead.

self.next = NextPort(send=TensorSpec((32, 256)), initial=torch.full((32, 256), 0.5))

Values on two ports travel independently: a reader may see a new value on one port with an old value on the other.

Send values that belong together (an input and its target, say) as one message: describe it with a TypedDict and a DictSpec, which gives a TensorSpec for each key. The whole dict arrives at once, and type checkers know the type of each key.

class Sample(TypedDict):
    x: torch.Tensor
    y: torch.Tensor


SAMPLE = DictSpec(Sample, x=TensorSpec((32, 4)), y=TensorSpec((32, 2)))

self.next = NextPort(send=SAMPLE)  # in the sender: self.next.send({"x": x, "y": y})
self.prev = PrevPort(recv=SAMPLE)  # in the receiver: sample = self.prev.recv(); sample["x"]

Type checkers infer the type of a port from its specs, so you seldom write it. To annotate one (an argument of a helper, say), write Port[S, R, M].

  • S is the type it sends
  • R the type it receives
  • M its number of peers, Single or Multi from mujou.typing

An omitted direction is Never. A function that takes any spec takes a MessageSpec[T] from mujou.typing.

from typing import Never

from mujou.typing import MessageSpec, Multi


def mean_of(port: PrevPort[Never, torch.Tensor, Multi]) -> torch.Tensor:
    return torch.stack(list(port.recv().values())).mean(0)


def sender[T](spec: MessageSpec[T]) -> NextPort[T, Never, Multi]:
    return NextPort(send=spec)

docs.title: 2. Set up the state in on_start
docs.text:
Create the state tensors in on_start.

Update the state in place

In on_update, do not assign a new tensor to the attribute; update the tensor in place with +=, copy_ and the like.

Assigning a new tensor raises no error, and the new tensor goes into the state under the same name. What breaks is any other reference to the tensor created in on_start (from an optimizer, another attribute, ...): it still points at the old tensor, and later updates do not reach it.

Updating in place keeps every reference on the one tensor. Restoring a state also writes in place into that tensor.

torch.Tensor and nn.Module values assigned to attributes are collected into the state automatically. What is collected, and how to save it, is in Saving and restoring state.

When the node computes on a GPU, create the tensors with device=self.device.

@override
def on_start(self) -> None:
    self.w = torch.zeros(256, 256, device=self.device)

You may keep settings (a time constant, the size of a layer, ...) as numbers set in __init__. Numbers are not collected into the state.

Build nn.Modules in on_start too, like the tensors of the state, because self.generator, the node's own generator for initialization, exists from on_start on. Built in __init__, a module such as nn.Linear is initialized from the global generator that all nodes share, so seed does not reproduce it.

docs.title: 3. Update in proportion to dt in on_update(dt)
docs.text:
Mujou calls on_update(dt) again and again. The node's author does not write a loop; write the work of one call only. One call does the following, in this order.

  1. Read the neighbors' latest values with recv(). It never waits for a new value to arrive
  2. Update the state by an amount proportional to dt
  3. Send the result with send()

dt is the time in seconds since this node's previous update. The first dt counts from when the run's timer starts, after every node's on_start (in a restored run, from the node's last update before the state was taken).

For a differential equation \(\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x)\), write x += dt * f(x) (explicit Euler). If the update size is not proportional to dt, a node that loops faster changes faster (see Global time).

dt is not constant. It gets longer when the machine is busy. Write on_update so that it does not diverge even with the longest dt that can come.

Do not cut dt

Do not cut dt itself. The time you cut off is lost, and the result drifts from the continuous-time solution.

There are two ways to update stably with a long dt.

  • Exact solution: if the system has an exact solution, advance the state by dt with that solution. The Leaky above does not use explicit Euler. It moves \(x\) by the fraction 1 - exp(-dt / tau) of its distance to \(u\). This fraction is exact while the input stays constant. It is below 1 for any dt, so \(x\) never overshoots \(u\)
  • Split the step: if the system has no exact solution, split the step inside one call of on_update. Choose n so that one step dt / n is no longer than a length that updates stably, and update n times in a for loop (see the example in PyTorch in nodes)

recv() always returns a value, and on_update usually runs more often than the peer sends, so the same message is read many times. That is right for a value that holds over time (a sensor reading, an activity): update toward it by dt each time.

For noise in a continuous-time update, scale its standard deviation by \(\sqrt{dt}\), not by dt, so that the result does not depend on how often the node updates.

When a message is an event to handle once (a training sample, say), read its time with recv_with_time() and skip the update while the time has not changed.

Until the peer first sends, recv() returns the port's initial value (zeros unless the sender declares initial=), and has_received() returns False: skip that value too. For a port the host writes, the inputs= value and each run.write count as sent.

In a restored run, has_received() returns True for a value that had been sent when the state was taken. self.last starts again from None, so the node handles that value once more (usually it was handled before the state was taken).

@override
def on_start(self) -> None:
    super().on_start()
    self.last: mujou.time.Timestamp | None = None  # the time of the last one handled


@override
def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
    super().on_update(dt)
    if not self.prev.has_received():  # the initial value: the peer has not sent yet
        return
    sample, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
    if t == self.last:  # nothing new since the last update
        return
    self.last = t
    ...  # learn from the sample once

docs.title: Set the period
docs.text:
A node updates once every period seconds on average, 0.01 s (100 times a second) by default. To match the period of a sensor, or to respond faster or slower, pass a period period in seconds.

class Sensor(mujou.Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=0.05)  # update once every 50 ms on average
        self.next = mujou.NextPort(send=mujou.TensorSpec((3,)))

The period is the average interval between updates. The time on_update takes counts as part of the period. A node that falls behind does not update several times in a row to catch up.

The wait is measured on the run's timer. If you change the time scale, the period changes by the same factor against real time.

Even with a period, dt is not exactly period. dt is the time that actually passed: after a delay it is longer than period, and the next one is shorter. Even with a period, update in proportion to dt.

In a pipeline fed by a node with a period (a sensor, say), the nodes after it read the same input until the next one arrives. Give them a period no longer than the period of their input.

period=0.0 uses up a CPU core

period=0.0 calls the next on_update as soon as any time has passed. Such a node uses up one CPU core, takes time from the other nodes and makes their dt irregular. Pass it only to a node that really must not wait.

Pass period only as an argument of super().__init__. Setting a default with a class attribute period = 0.01 makes the start of the run raise TypeError.

A manual run (see Testing) does not use the period.

docs.title: Set the seed and the device
docs.text:
super().__init__ takes the following arguments. All of them are keyword arguments and can be left out.

Argument Meaning Default device The device the node computes on. "cpu" or a CUDA device "cpu" seed The seed of the node's own random number generator self.generator None (different every time) period The period of updates, in seconds 0.01

Draw random numbers from self.generator (torch.randn(..., generator=self.generator)). Do not call torch.manual_seed in a node, because it changes the random number generator that all nodes share.

self.generator can be used in the hooks from on_start on. How it works with PyTorch is in PyTorch in nodes.

device, generator, period and timer are reserved names. Do not assign attributes with these names.

docs.title: The hooks and their order
docs.text:
Mujou calls the hooks of a node in this order. Override only the ones you need.

  1. on_thread_start(): once, before on_start. Per-thread settings (see PyTorch in nodes)
  2. on_start(): once. Create the state
  3. load_state_dict(state): once, only when the run is restored (see Saving and restoring state)
  4. on_update(dt): again and again until the run ends
  5. on_pause() and on_resume(): before and after the run's state is taken. state_dict() is called between them
  6. on_exception(): once on every node, when any hook of any node raises (see Errors and shutdown)
  7. on_stop(): once at the end, normal or not

docs.title: What not to do in a hook
docs.text:
Do not Why, and what happens Wait for another node's value to change (repeat recv() in a loop, ...) Nodes do not wait for each other. If a value has not changed, the node goes on with the same value Call mujou.run or a method of Run (write, read, state_dict, ...) It raises RuntimeError. A node talks only through its own ports Call an operation that moves the time, such as mujou.time.sleep or set_time_scale It raises RuntimeError. Only the host moves the time Call backward() across nodes A sent value is detached from the computation graph, so gradients do not pass through a port Write a loop that never returns from on_update Pausing, ending and taking the state stop working. Mujou owns the loop. A finite for loop that splits the step is fine

To know the time, read the time of the run's timer with self.timer.now(). Reading it is allowed in a hook.

If any hook raises, the whole network stops (see Errors and shutdown).

docs.text:
連続的継続学習のための非同期分散型深層学習フレームワーク

画像は、落合陽一の作品「リキッドユニバース」をもとに新たに制作したもの

mujou は推論と学習を同時に行い続ける深層学習フレームワークである。ノードをつなぎ、ネットワークを構築する。

開発の初期段階

mujou はまだ開発の初期段階にある。API は予告なく変わることがある。

docs.title: 🌱 学び続けるネットワーク
docs.text:
従来の機械学習は学習を終えたら重みを固定し推論する。mujou のネットワークは、実行中常に入力を受け取って出力を出し、同時に学び続ける。

学習と推論を切り替えるモードも、エポックも無い。

名前は「諸行無常」の「無常」（常が無いこと）から取った。ストリームから学び続け、常に変わり続ける機械を作るためのフレームワーク。リアルタイム処理やロボティクスのように、動きながら学ぶ用途を狙う。

docs.title: ✨ 特徴
docs.text:
• 🔄 推論と学習を同時に: 学習のモードも推論のモードも、エポックも無い
  • 🧩 PyTorch で書くノード: 各ノードは PyTorch で書き実行する
  • ⚡ 非同期のノード: 各ノードは自分のスレッドで更新し、ほかのノードを待たない
  • ⏱️ 連続時間: 実際に経った時間 dt に比例して更新する
  • 💾 状態を保存: ネットワークの状態を取得、後でその状態からリスタート
  • 🧪 決定的なテスト: 仮想のタイマーと手動の更新でノードをテスト可能

docs.title: ⚙️ 動き方
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    H["ホスト（あなたのプログラム）"] -->|"入力を書く"| A["ノード A"]
    A -->|"最新の値"| B["ノード B"]
    B -->|"出力を読む"| H

各ノードは自分のスレッドで更新を繰り返し、ほかのノードを待たない。読むのは、隣のノードが最後に送った値である。

ホスト（ネットワークを走らせるプログラム）は、走っているネットワークに入力を書き、出力を読む。

docs.title: 🚀 最小のプログラム
docs.text:
次のプログラムは、2 つのノードで \(y = 2x + 1\) を計算するネットワークを走らせ、出力を読む。何をしているかはクイックスタートで説明する。

examples/quickstart.py 
"""The smallest program: two nodes in a network, run in the background.

The host writes an input, follows the output until it arrives and stops.
"""

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((3,))  # every message here is a float32 vector of 3


class Scale(Node):
    """Sends its input times ``factor``."""

    def __init__(self, factor: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.factor = factor
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous side
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next side

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # the latest input; never waits
        self.next.send(self.factor * x)


class Shift(Node):
    """Sends its input plus ``offset``."""

    def __init__(self, offset: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.offset = offset
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.prev.recv() + self.offset)


class Affine(mujou.Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Scale(2.0)
        self.shift = Shift(1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev = self.scale.prev  # the input of the network
        self.next = self.shift.next  # the output of the network




net = Affine()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on threads of their own until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})  # the unconnected input port of scale
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
assert torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1)

docs.title: 🧠 Mujou の仕組み
docs.text:
mujou の考え方を、次の 5 つに分けて説明する。

  • ノード: 計算の単位
  • Port と Channel: ノード同士をつなぐ口と接続
  • ネットワーク: ノードの組み合わせ方
  • グローバル時間: すべてのノードが従う時間の流れ
  • 状態: 実行中のネットワークから取得し、後で復元できるもの

コードの書き方はユーザーガイドを参照。

flowchart TB
    H["ホスト（ネットワークを動かす Python のコード）"]
    subgraph N["ネットワーク"]
        direction LR
        A["ノード A"] <-->|Channel| B["ノード B"] <-->|Channel| C["ノード C"]
    end
    T["実行のタイマー"]
    H -->|"mujou.run(net) が返す Run で、入力を書き、出力を読み、状態を取得する"| N
    T -.->|"時刻と dt"| N

docs.title: ノード
docs.text:
ノードは計算の単位で、mujou.Node を継承したクラスとして書く。

ノードの内側では PyTorch のコードを同期的に実行する。ノードの内側に閉じていれば誤差逆伝播法（BP）も使える。

ノード同士はすべて非同期に動く。mujou はノードごとのスレッドで on_update(dt) を繰り返し呼び、ノードはほかのノードを待たない。on_update のたびにノードは次のことをする。

  1. 隣のノードが送った最新の値を読む
  2. 自分の状態を更新する
  3. 結果を送る

ループは mujou が回すので、ノードは自分で while ループを持たない。実行の開始時や終了時などにも、mujou はノードが override できる hook を呼ぶ。呼ばれる順は API リファレンスの Node を参照。

エポックも、学習と推論の切り替えも、メッセージを受け取るたびに呼ばれる hook も無い。

1 つのノードにどれだけの計算を入れるかはノードのクラスで決まる。1 つの層でも、複数の層でも、モデル全体でもよい。ノードの境界がそのまま非同期の境界になる。複数の層を同期的に計算したいときや、BP で一緒に学習させたいときは、それらを 1 つのノードのクラスにまとめる。

ノードが守る 3 つの規則

  • 計算グラフをつなげない: ノードをまたいで計算グラフをつなげない。送った値は送信時に計算グラフから切り離されるので、勾配はノード間を通らない
  • Port だけでやり取りする: ほかのノードやホストとは自分の Port だけでやり取りする
  • 時間は読むだけ: 時間を動かせるのはホストだけ

どれかのノードが例外を投げると実行全体が止まる。例外を投げたノードだけを止め、ほかのノードを動かし続けることはない（例外と終了）。

既定の更新手法は PC-ALM（Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding。実装予定）で、各ノードは局所的な更新だけで学ぶ。更新手法は mujou に組み込まれていないので、上の 3 つを守る限りノードはどの手法でも使える。

docs.title: Port と Channel
docs.text:
Port はノードが持つ接続口である。Channel は 2 つの Port をつなぐ 1 本の接続で、connect で作る。

Channel は向きごとに値の置き場所を 1 つずつ持ち、各置き場所に書けるのはその向きの送り手だけである。

Port は送る値と受け取る値の型を shape と dtype で宣言する。互いの送る型が相手の受け取る型と一致するときだけ、2 つの Port は接続できる。この検査は connect を呼んだときに mujou が行う。dtype は変換しない。

読み書きの動作は次のとおり。

  • 待たない: 読む側はその時点の最新の値を受け取る。新しい値が来るまで待つことはない
  • 溜まらない: 誰にも読まれないまま上書きされる値もあれば、同じ値を何度も読むこともある。どちらも正常な動作
  • 初期値: 送り手がまだ書いていなければ、送り手の Port の初期値（既定はゼロ）を読む。送り手が書いたかどうかは has_received() でわかる
  • コピー: 値はどれも計算グラフから切り離された torch.Tensor のコピー。受け取ったテンソルを書き換えても、ほかのノードには影響しない
  • 時刻付き: 値には送った時刻が付く。新しい値かどうかは、値を時刻と一緒に読み（recv_with_time()）、前回読んだ値の時刻と比べればわかる。時刻が進んでいれば新しい値

1 つの Port を複数の相手に接続することもできる。その場合は Channel ごとに値を 1 つずつ受け取り、それらをどう束ねるか（足す、平均するなど）はノードが決める。

どこにも接続していない Port を残してもよい。接続していない Port がネットワークの入力と出力になる。

  • ホストは接続していない入力の Port に入力を書く。書いた値はホストが次に書くまでその Port に残る
  • ホストは値を送るどの Port からも、送られた最新の値を読める。接続していない出力の Port だけでなく、ノード同士をつなぐ Port も読める

docs.title: ネットワーク
docs.text:
ネットワークはノードの組み合わせ方を宣言するもので、mujou.Network を継承したクラスとして書く。PyTorch の nn.Module に子のモジュールを持たせるのと同じ書き方で、次の 3 段階で組む。

  1. ノードや別のネットワークを属性として持つ
  2. それらの Port を connect でつなぐ
  3. 外からつなぎたい Port をネットワーク自身の属性として公開する

Port を公開したネットワークは、ノードと同じようにほかのノードやネットワークと接続できる。

ネットワークを使うのは組み立てるときだけである。ネットワークは hook を持たず、自身では何も実行しない。実行中も中のノードはそれぞれ独立に動き、ネットワークで囲んでも同期はしない。

mujou.run(net) は構造と型を検査し、凍結してから走らせる。その後は接続を足せない。

各ノードにはパスという名前が付く。パスはルートからの属性名を . でつないだもので、"body.l1" のようになる。状態ではこのパスを使う。

名前や接続を変えると状態を復元できない

属性の名前や接続を変えると、変える前に取得した状態は復元できなくなる。

docs.title: グローバル時間
docs.text:
mujou は学習するネットワークを、時間とともに連続的に変わる系として扱う。dt はそのノードの前回の更新からの経過時間（秒）である。

ノードは状態を dt に比例して更新する。状態 \(x\) が \(\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x)\) に従うなら、1 回の更新は次のようになる（陽的 Euler 法）。

x = x + dt * f(x)

更新の速さはノードごとに違い、負荷によっても揺らぐ。更新量を反復 1 回あたりで決めると、速く回るノードほど状態が大きく変わってしまう。dt に比例させれば、どのノードも同じ時間の流れの上で同じダイナミクスに従う。負荷が高くなっても dt が伸びるだけで済む。

dt を打ち切らない

dt に上限を設けて打ち切ってはならない。打ち切ると実際に経った時間が失われる。dt が大きくて更新が不安定になるなら、1 回の on_update の中で刻みを分割する。

ノードは周期を持つ（既定は 0.01 秒）。更新の間隔は 1 回ごとに揺らぐが、平均すると周期ごとに 1 回更新する。遅れたときの dt は周期より長くなる。dt は実際に経った時間なので、周期を決めていても更新は dt に比例させる。

タイマーは実行ごとに 1 つあり、その実行のすべてのノードとホストがそれを使う。既定ではプロセスに 1 つのグローバルタイマーを使う。ホストは時間を実時間より速くも遅くも進められるが、ノードは時間を読むだけである。

ホストは mujou.time.sleep で待つ

ホストがその時間で待つとき（たとえば入力を 2 秒見せるとき）は mujou.time.sleep を使う。標準の time.sleep は実時間で待つので使わない。

実行中のネットワークの状態を取得するとき、mujou は実行を一時停止してそのタイマーを止める。止まっていた時間は再開後のどの dt にも入らないので、ノードから見ると一時停止は無かったのと同じである。

一時停止は同じタイマーを使うすべての実行の時間を止める。ほかの実行と時間を止め合わないようにするには、その実行に専用のタイマーを持たせる（時間の制御）。

一時停止は状態の取得と観測のためのもので、学習の手順の一部にしてはならない。

docs.title: 状態
docs.text:
実行中のネットワークの状態は、実行を終了させずに取得でき、後でその状態から再開できる。状態は 1 つの木で、次のものを持つ。

  • ノードのパスごとの、各ノードの状態（重み、活動などのテンソル）
  • 値の置き場所ごとの、最新の値とその時刻
  • 各ノードの最後の更新の時刻と、タイマーの時刻

ネットワークはノードとその間を流れる値を合わせたものなので、置き場所の値も状態に含める。置き場所の値が初期値に戻ると、隣のノードはそれまでにたどり着いた平衡から外れてしまう。

ノードは nn.Module と同じように自分の状態を自分で集める。属性に代入したテンソルと nn.Module は自動で状態に入る。

状態を取得する間は、前の節で述べた一時停止が起きる。各ノードは on_update の途中では止まらず、1 回の更新を終えてから次の更新を始めるまでの間で止まる。そのため木の中の値はすべて同じ時点のものになる。

状態を取得するとき 得られるもの ネットワークの実行中 その時点の状態 正常に終了した後 on_stop の後にノードが残した値 例外で終了した後 取得できず NetworkError になる。残したい状態は実行中に取得しておく

正常に終了した後の木が持つタイマーの時刻は、shutdown() が終了を求めた時刻と、ノードが最後に更新か送信をした時刻のうち遅いほうである。この木から復元した実行は、終了した後に経った時間を数えない。

on_stop で状態を変えない

正常に終了した後の木は on_stop の後に取得するので、on_stop で状態を変えるとその変更が木に入る。たとえば on_stop で self.w = None とすると、木から w が消える。on_stop では状態を変えず、I/O などの資源だけを解放する。

復元するには、木を mujou.run(net, state=tree) に渡す。ネットワークは木を取得した時刻から、同じノードの状態と置き場所の値で続きを走る。走らせるネットワークは、木を取得したネットワークと同じノードのパスと接続を持たなければならない。

木をファイルに保存する方法（torch.save、pickle など）は利用者が決める。手順は状態の保存と復元を参照。

  • branching.py: 1 つの NextPort から複数のノードへ送り、PrevPort(multi=True) で合流して受け取る。send_to を使うと、connect が返した Channel の相手にだけ送れる
  • group.py: Group(enc=..., dec=...) と mujou.run(a, b)。ノードのパス（"enc.scale"、"0.scale"）の付き方
  • save_and_restore.py: run.state_dict() で状態を取得し、テンソルを CPU に移して torch.save で保存し、mujou.run(..., state=...) で復元して続ける
  • pause.py: mujou.time.pause() でグローバルタイマーを止め、そのタイマーで走る 2 つの実行の状態を同じ時刻で取得してから mujou.time.resume() で再開する。一方の状態から復元した実行は、その時刻から続く
  • subscribe.py: run.subscribe でまずその時点の最新の出力を受け取り、その後はより新しい出力が送られるたびに最新の 1 つを受け取る。受け取る前に次の値が送られると途中の値は飛ばされる。20 個受け取ったら break でループを抜ける
  • online_learning.py: 教師のノードが、ホストの書く a を使って y = a x + b のバッチを 10 ms ごとに送る。ホストは実行の途中で a を変える。学習するノードは新しいバッチごとに 1 回学び、学習と推論の段階を分けない。ホストは学習するノードの損失を run.wait_for で追う。損失は下がり、目標が変わると跳ね上がり、学習するノードが追いつくとまた下がる
  • torch_node.py: ノードの中の nn.Module を、ノードの内側に閉じた BP で学習させる。シードの指定と、dt を刻みに分けて進める更新
  • testing_a_node.py: mujou.testing の仮想タイマーと手動の更新で、ノードを決まった dt と順序で動かし、結果を参照の計算とビット単位で比べる。途中で取得した状態から復元した実行が、止めずに続けた実行と一致することも確かめる
  • timers.py: 時刻 Timestamp、実行ごとのタイマー Timer、時間の速さ（実行のタイマーとグローバルタイマー）
  • errors.py: ホストが受け取る NetworkError とその __cause__、on_exception → on_stop の順、on_start の例外は mujou.run が送出する

もの 条件 Python 3.14 以上。free-threaded 版の 3.14t を推奨。GIL ありでも良い。 PyTorch mujou の依存として自動でインストールされる Rust 1.85 以上を rustup でインストール。ソースからのビルド用 uv uv。ソースからのビルド用

各ノードは自分のスレッドで動くので、free-threaded 版を勧める。GIL ありの版では Python で書いたノード同士が GIL を取り合い、並列に動きにくい。

git clone https://github.com/Geson-anko/mujou.git
cd mujou
uv sync

uv sync は free-threaded 版の Python 3.14t を用意して .venv/ を作り、依存をインストールし、Rust で書かれたコアをビルドする。GIL ありの通常版を使うなら、代わりに uv sync --python 3.14 を実行する。

PyTorch はほかの依存と同じく PyPI からインストールされる。CPU 版や別の CUDA 版を使いたい場合は PyTorch のインストール案内を参照。

PyPI に公開した後

公開後は、uv のプロジェクトなら uv add mujou、pip なら Python 3.14 以上の仮想環境で pip install mujou でインストールできるようになる。

2 つ目のプログラムとその出力についてはクイックスタートで説明する。

docs.title: 🚀 クイックスタート
docs.text:
最小のプログラムを走らせてみる。2 つのノードをつないで \(y = 2x + 1\) を計算するプログラムである。

flowchart LR
    H1["ホスト"] -->|"x を書く"| S["scale（2 倍）"]
    S --> F["shift（+1）"]
    F -->|"y を読む"| H2["ホスト"]

docs.title: プログラム
docs.text:
examples/quickstart.py
"""The smallest program: two nodes in a network, run in the background.

The host writes an input, follows the output until it arrives and stops.
"""

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NextPort, Node, PrevPort, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((3,))  # every message here is a float32 vector of 3


class Scale(Node):
    """Sends its input times ``factor``."""

    def __init__(self, factor: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.factor = factor
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous side
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next side

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # the latest input; never waits
        self.next.send(self.factor * x)


class Shift(Node):
    """Sends its input plus ``offset``."""

    def __init__(self, offset: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.offset = offset
        self.prev = PrevPort(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = NextPort(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.prev.recv() + self.offset)


class Affine(mujou.Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Scale(2.0)
        self.shift = Shift(1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev = self.scale.prev  # the input of the network
        self.next = self.shift.next  # the output of the network




net = Affine()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on threads of their own until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})  # the unconnected input port of scale
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
assert torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1)

リポジトリのルートで次のように実行する。

uv run python examples/quickstart.py

次のような 1 行が表示される。

y = tensor([3., 5., 7.]) at t = 0.017 s

y は x = [1, 2, 3] に対する \(2x + 1\) である。t は shift が y を送った時刻で、単位は mujou のグローバル時間の秒。t の値は実行ごとに変わる。

docs.title: 何が起きたか
docs.text:
• Scale と Shift は mujou.Node を継承したノード。それぞれ __init__ で Port を宣言し、1 回分の処理を on_update(dt) に書く。どのサブクラスとも同じく、最初に super().__init__() と super().on_update(dt) を呼ぶ
  • Affine はネットワーク。ノードを属性として持ち、その Port 同士を connect でつなぐ。どこにも接続していない scale の prev を入力として、shift の next を出力として公開する
  • mujou.run(net) はノードを動かし始め、ノードが動き出すと戻る。各ノードは自分のスレッドで on_update を繰り返す。on_update の中の recv() は待たずに最新の値を読むので、x が scale を通り抜けるまで shift は前の入力（最初はゼロ）から計算した値を送り続ける
  • そのため run.write の直後に読んだ出力はまだ古いことがある。run.write で x を書き、出力が条件を満たすまで run.wait_for で待つ。実時間で 5 秒たっても満たさなければ TimeoutError になる。with ブロックを抜けるとネットワークが止まる
